title: Crisis hits Nigeria’s cassava industry with imports rising 13,293% in 5yrs
description:
*… as Farmers Abandon Farms in 2026







By Cynthia Alo



Nigeria’s cassava processing industry is facing a deepening crisis as imports of cassava starch surged by 13,293 per cent in five years, leaving local factories struggling, farmers counting their losses and processors operating at low 15 p
content:
*… as Farmers Abandon Farms in 2026

By Cynthia Alo

Nigeria’s cassava processing industry is facing a deepening crisis as imports of cassava starch surged by 13,293 per cent in five years, leaving local factories struggling, farmers counting their losses and processors operating at low 15 per cent of their installed capacity.

This is happening despite Nigeria’s position as the world’s largest cassava producer as of 2024, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database, FAOSTAT, an agency of the United Nations.

Industry stakeholders attributed the crisis to high production costs, inadequate financing, declining farm acreage and weak enforcement of import restrictions. These factors have made imported alternatives cheaper than locally produced cassava derivatives.

The situation has resulted in a glut of raw cassava, falling farm-gate prices, mounting debts among farmers and processors, and growing concerns about the future of local industrial production.

Data obtained from the World Bank’s World Integrated Trade Solution, WITS, based on UN Comtrade records, showed that Nigeria’s cassava starch imports rose from 24.1 tonnes in 2020 to 3,227.7 tonnes in 2025, representing a 13,293 per cent increase over five years.

A year-on-year breakdown showed that Nigeria imported 24.1 tonnes of cassava starch, valued at $69,440, in 2020.

Imports increased by 126.6 per cent year-on-year (YoY) in 2021 to 54.6 tonnes, worth $154,750. In 2022, the volume surged by a further 272.2 per cent YoY to 203.2 tonnes, valued at $292,900.

However, following a sharp rise in the exchange rate, imports plunged by 98 per cent YoY in 2023 to 4.1 tonnes, valued at $32,080, before rebounding sharply in 2024 by 73,004.9 per cent to 2,997.3 tonnes, worth $2.34 million.

The upward trend continued in 2025, with import volumes rising by 7.7 per cent to 3,227.7 tonnes. However, despite the increase in volume, the value of imports declined by 7.6 per cent to $2.16 million from approximately $2.34 million in 2024.

Industry stakeholders, who spoke in exclusive interviews with Financial Vanguard, warned that imports were rising further in 2026 and could continue to increase in subsequent years unless the government addressed the cost disadvantages confronting local processors and strengthened policies supporting domestic production.

Farmers, processors count losses

The President of Large-Scale Starch and Derivatives Producers Association of Nigeria, LSSDPA, Mrs Oluyemisi Iranloye, who is also the Vice-President of the Industrial Cassava Stakeholders Association of Nigeria, ICSAN, said the crisis had severely affected farmers and processors.

Iranloye, founder and Chief Executive Officer of Psaltry International, said farmers could spend about N800,000 cultivating a hectare of cassava but realise only about N300,000 from selling the produce at prevailing farm-gate prices.

She said the situation had discouraged farmers from planting, while industrial processors, which ordinarily absorb substantial quantities of cassava, were scaling down operations because of weak demand.

Illustrating crisis severity in the processing industry, she said: “As you speak right now, factories that should be generating about N10 billion a year are barely generating N1 billion. Factories are running at about 15 per cent capacity because there’s no market.

“The market that is available is flooded by importation. So factories are dying, people cannot pay up their loans. We buy from smallholder farmers, and when we are not buying, smallholder farmers cannot sell, and the implication is that everybody suffers.

“What we have witnessed over the last 18 to 20 months is particularly troubling. Several processing companies have either reduced their operations, struggled to maintain production or become less active in the market.

“Consequently, the volume of cassava that would ordinarily have been absorbed by industrial processors has increasingly remained within the traditional food market, putting considerable pressure on farm-gate prices.”

Iranloye warned that the situation could also threaten future cassava supplies as farmers become increasingly reluctant to invest in cultivation when they cannot recover their production costs.

She said the solution laid in addressing the broader production and supply-chain constraints.

“We must also invest in the agricultural supply base, mechanisation, improved planting materials, aggregation centres, transportation and alternative energy solutions,” she said.

Tariff favours imports

Explaining the factors behind the growing dependence on imported starch, Iranloye said the current tariff structure had made imported corn starch and pharmaceutical-grade starch cheaper than locally produced cassava starch.

According to her, the reduction in tariffs on competing products, such as corn starch and pharmaceutical-grade starch, had made imported alternatives more competitive than locally produced cassava starch

She said: “I believe this report, the imports will increase in 2026 because the import duty is still supporting cassava starch and corn starch, a situation that large-scale starch and its derivative producers have been fighting.

“Now, the situation is that the tariff on corn starch used to be about 15 per cent some four years ago, and at that point, we were able to compete because we had some form of little protection.

“But right now, the tariff on corn starch and pharmaceutical-grade starch were reduced to five per cent. What it means is that they can bring it in cheaper than what we are producing.

“So, the multinationals that usually buy from us, the large-scale starch factories in Nigeria, are now importing, landing cheaper than our cost of production, so they now import thousands of containers, and they now buy very little locally.

“The implication is that we are also not buying much cassava from farmers, so prices have crashed below what the farmers can handle, and that’s why we have the glut right now.”

Iranloye said pharmaceutical-grade starch was also being brought into Nigeria under zero-duty arrangements, with some importers allegedly importing quantities beyond their immediate requirements and selling the excess in the local market.

She said: “Another point is pharmaceutical-grade starch also finds its way into Nigeria. So pharmaceutical companies are importing pharmaceutical-grade starch into Nigeria at zero duty.

“But instead of just importing the quantity that they require alone, they import more and sell also to the local market.

“So we have been fighting the importation heavily, yet we have more than 30 factories not running well, cassava not being bought, there’s glut because of tariff mismatch.”

The Federal Government’s Executive Order on Increasing Local Production of Healthcare Products provides import-duty and VAT exemptions for specified pharmaceutical raw materials.

The official list of exempted materials specifically includes pharmaceutical-grade corn starch under HS Code 1108121000.

Farmers warn of further supply decline

Meanwhile, food security expert and farmer, Mr Africanfarmer Mogaji, said Nigeria could continue to experience increased importation in 2026, particularly through less-publicised channels, if government policies remained inconsistent.

Mogaji said Nigeria had significantly expanded its cassava processing capacity over the past decade, particularly as foreign exchange pressures made imports more expensive and encouraged manufacturers to source raw materials locally.

However, he said many farmers and processors who invested during that period are now heavily indebted following changes in market conditions.

He said: “The processors have increased capacity by taking loans because of the demand previously. The farmers have taken loans, taken too much risk, over-exposed themselves.

“And now it is cheaper to import cassava starch from Thailand because the government of that country has heavily invested in infrastructure from raw material to inputs to logistics.

“So many of the multinationals have over-imported and they are not taking the starch from the Nigerian processors, and so the processors also cannot take cassava from the local farmers.”

Mogaji said some multinational companies had taken advantage of import windows to bring in quantities beyond their immediate requirements, thereby weakening demand for locally produced cassava derivatives.

He said the impact could persist beyond 2026 because some manufacturers had already secured imported supplies for an extended period.

He said: “They’ve secured themselves mostly till the end of 2027 and first quarter 2028.

“So Nigerians will feel it on their table again. And so whatever government is trying to do to tighten up to support local production will be a waste.”

Mogaji said Nigeria needs a long-term agricultural policy framework that will enable farmers and processors to plan beyond individual administrations.

He said: “If we don’t have policies that can last an average of 10 years in the pilot stage, we’re not going anywhere.

“But we can convert and focus on food, maybe cassava to fufu, cassava to garri, cassava to paste, cassava to many other products that people can consume at scale.

“I’m optimistic there’s still room for the private sector, but over-dependence on government would not work.”

Farmers reduce acreage as costs rise

Similarly, the Managing Director of Niji Group, Mr Kolawole Adeniji, said the projected increase in imports in 2026 will also be driven by a decline in cassava farming activities this year.

Adeniji, who has more than 36 years of experience in agriculture and operates a cassava farm covering more than 4,000 acres, said farmers were reducing farm sizes because of the high costs of machinery, diesel and transportation, insecurity, and poor returns on cassava cultivation.

He said: “The import will increase next year because a lot of people are not farming this year. Farmers have reduced the acreage of their farm sizes due to the implements and the cost of tractors, insecurity, then the poor market for what they have planted over a period of three years.

“So a lot of people are not doing any serious farming this year. The cost of diesel is very high, so the cost of transportation is very high. The cost of selling tractors, when you look at all the factors surrounding the production, people are not farming the way they should. So it’s going to affect us next year.”

Adeniji also attributed Nigeria’s dependence on imported starch to the high cost of producing and processing cassava locally, saying farmers and processors faced expenses that producers in competing countries do not bear to the same extent.

He said: “Most of the farmers who are practising are not making profit because the supporting system is not properly structured.”

According to him, imported starch, including potato and maize starch, can also be cheaper than locally produced cassava starch because of differences in infrastructure, energy and production costs.

He said: “Immediately the government opened the border to bring starch, the cost of producing potato starch and everything is cheaper than what you produce in Nigeria.”

Adeniji also said cassava processing required long-term financing, arguing that farmers and processors could not operate sustainably with short-term loans.

He said: “If the government wants to provide loans, it must be almost a three year cycle.”

Processing capacity struggles despite investment

Despite the challenges, industry records showed that Nigeria has developed significant cassava processing capacity over the years.

A June 18, 2026, document obtained by Vanguard from the Large-Scale Starch and Derivatives Producers Association listed 62 cassava processor entries affiliated with the association, including processors registered with ICSAN.

The records showed that 55 entries were engaged in starch and high-quality cassava flour, HQCF, processing, with a combined listed daily capacity of 1,662.5 tonnes, while seven ethanol-related processors had a combined recorded capacity of 1.073 million litres daily.

Among the companies listed for starch and HQCF production were Psaltry International Limited, Dufil Prima Foods Limited, GreenTech Industries Limited, Harvest Feed and Agro Processing Limited, Niji Industries Limited, Acsmin Cassava Industries and Premium Cassava Product Limited.

The ethanol processors included Green Hills Agricultural Products, Premier Plantations Limited, Weewood Industries Limited, Allied Atlantic Distilleries Limited, Pure Biotech Company Limited, Unicane Industries Limited and Arog BioAllied Agro Services Limited.

However, the association noted that some companies might not be operating at full capacity because of challenges, while some companies, including those operated by Chinese investors, were not captured in the list.

Production versus industrial use

The concerns come despite Nigeria’s position as the world’s largest cassava producer.

Data from the Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database, FAOSTAT, released in 2025, showed that Nigeria accounted for about 18 per cent of global cassava output in 2024, ahead of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ghana, while national production had risen to more than 63 million tonnes.

However, the country’s large production volume has not translated into commensurate industrial utilisation.

Speaking at the 10th anniversary of ICSAN in Lagos, its President, Mr Segun Ladele, said only about five per cent of Nigeria’s cassava output currently goes into industrial use, with the bulk consumed as food or exported.

He said: “About 80 per cent is consumed locally as food, five per cent goes into industry and about 15 per cent for export. So when we are talking about industrialisation, there is still a lot of room to make improvements.”

title: ‘How Tinubu will end insecurity ready’
description:
By Dapo Akinrefon



ABUJA — THE All Progressives Congress APC, Presidential Campaign Council, APC-PCC, yesterday, unveiled President Bola Tinubu defence plan to end the 17-year scourge of insecurity ravaging parts of Nigeria through a comprehensive five-year strategic defence operations plan.



Re
content:
By Dapo Akinrefon

ABUJA — THE All Progressives Congress APC, Presidential Campaign Council, APC-PCC, yesterday, unveiled President Bola Tinubu defence plan to end the 17-year scourge of insecurity ravaging parts of Nigeria through a comprehensive five-year strategic defence operations plan.

Read Also: Igini to Trump: Tie Nigeria-US relations to credible polls

The APC-PCC said the plan is designed to strengthen the country’s security architecture, improve military effectiveness, and ensure a coordinated response to emerging threats.

Spokesperson of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Dele Alake, who disclosed this in a statement, said the plan provided a long-term framework for aligning defence priorities, operational requirements, capability development, and expenditure with Nigeria’s current and anticipated security challenges.

He also said ongoing military operations across the country had led to the elimination of more than 15,000 Boko Haram terrorists and bandits, with more than 130,000 fighters and dependants of Boko Haram surrendering through Operation Safe Corridor.

Alaka said: “The initiative is a major component of President Tinubu’s determination to reposition the nation’s security architecture toward a more coordinated, intelligence-led, technology-enabled, and prevention-oriented system capable of addressing terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, and other forms of criminality.

“In the last three years, the scale of the administration’s ongoing military operations across the country has led to the elimination of more than 15,000 Boko Haram terrorists and bandits, with more than 130,000 fighters and dependants of Boko Haram having surrendered through Operation Safe Corridor, the Federal Government’s rehabilitation programme for repentant insurgents.

“The figures underscore the administration’s two-phase approach of sustained military operations and non-kinetic interventions to address insecurity.”

On the expansion of military formations, manpower, he said the plan would “strengthen the Nigerian Army’s operational capacity and improve responses to security threats.”

According to him, President Tinubu has created four new Army divisions and restructured existing military formations.

He added: “The reforms aim to expand operational coverage, decentralise military operations, and enable troops to respond more swiftly to security threats across the country.

“The President has also approved the establishment of two additional Army depots in Osogbo, Osun State, and in Amasiri-Edda, Ebonyi State, to expand military training capacity and accelerate the recruitment and training of new soldiers.

“Each depot can accommodate 6,000 recruits at a time, bringing their combined training capacity to 12,000 soldiers.

“The Osogbo facility’s capacity is already being demonstrated, with 5,210 recruits currently undergoing training there.

“The expansion of training facilities is expected to reduce recruit turnaround time and increase the number of soldiers available for deployment.

“To further the manpower expansion drive, President Tinubu also approved recruiting an additional 28,000 soldiers to strengthen the military’s presence on the ground and enhance its operational effectiveness.

“The President also approved recruiting 50,000 additional police officers as part of broader efforts to reinforce internal security, improve policing capacity, and strengthen the country’s response to criminal activities.

“Beyond investments in equipment, technology and training, the administration is also investing in military accommodation and operational infrastructure to improve personnel welfare and effectiveness.

“One such project is the 700-unit military barracks in Ikere-Ekiti, Ekiti State, designed to provide military personnel with a professional living and working environment and essential military infrastructure.

“The facilities are expected to provide the accommodation and operational support personnel need while strengthening the military’s capacity to maintain an effective presence in the area.

“These measures reflect the administration’s determination to address manpower and infrastructure gaps, improve the capacity of security agencies, and ensure personnel are adequately trained, equipped, and deployed to areas facing security challenges”, Alake said.

On intelligence, surveillance and coordination, the APC-PCC spokesperson said: “Under the Five-Year Strategic Defence Operations Plan, the federal government is adopting a more strategic approach to national defence by ensuring that investments in the security sector are guided by clearly identified threats, operational requirements and national priorities.

“The plan is expected to strengthen combat readiness, address critical capability gaps, optimise available resources and minimise unnecessary expenditure and wastage.”

title: Igini to Trump: Tie Nigeria-US relations to credible polls
description:
A former Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC,  Resident Electoral Commissioner, Mike Igini, has urged US President, Donald Trump, to link America’s immigration policy and diplomatic relations with Nigeria to credible conduct of the country’s 2027 general elections.



Read Also: ‘How Tin
content:
A former Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, Resident Electoral Commissioner, Mike Igini, has urged US President, Donald Trump, to link America’s immigration policy and diplomatic relations with Nigeria to credible conduct of the country’s 2027 general elections.

Read Also: ‘How Tinubu will end insecurity ready’  

Igini said electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and poor governance were among the factors forcing Nigerians to seek opportunities abroad, arguing that credible elections and accountable leadership could help address the root causes of migration.

In an open letter dated November 13, 2026, and addressed to Trump at the White House, the former REC proposed a policy he called the “No Mandate Fraud” Doctrine, urging the US to combine preventive diplomacy, independent election monitoring and targeted sanctions against individuals involved in electoral violations.

He argued that border enforcement alone could not address migration without tackling the governance failures driving Nigerians out of their country.

“Nigerians are not leaving Nigeria because they do not love their country. They are leaving because of decades of persistent electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and weak public accountability that have undermined Nigerians’ confidence in government,” he wrote.

Igini urged Trump to send a high-level delegation to engage President Bola Tinubu, political parties, presidential and governorship candidates, INEC and other relevant institutions ahead of the elections.

He said the delegation should communicate Washington’s position that credible elections, peaceful political competition and respect for constitutional rights were central to US interests in Nigeria.

He also proposed visa restrictions, financial sanctions and asset freezes, where legally justified, against electoral officials found culpable of manipulating results, falsifying records or committing other electoral offences.

The former REC extended the call for accountability to judicial officers whose misconduct in electoral cases was established by credible evidence, as well as security personnel involved in voter intimidation, electoral violence and suppression of opposition parties.

He identified the police, Department of State Services, Armed Forces and Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps as institutions expected to protect voters and ensure impartial enforcement of the law.

Igini further urged the US to support credible domestic and international election observers to monitor the process before, during and after the polls, particularly voter intimidation, security neutrality, polling-unit results and transparent collation.

Explaining the benefits to Washington, he said credible elections could reduce migration pressure, strengthen security cooperation and create opportunities for stronger economic relations.

He also identified potential US investment in Nigeria’s energy sector, particularly electricity development, through technology transfer and private-sector partnerships.

Warning against waiting for an electoral crisis before intervening, Igini said: “The time to act is before the election, not after a crisis has occurred.”

He urged Washington to make clear that it would not conduct business as usual with any government produced through electoral fraud, stressing that sanctions must be lawful and supported by credible evidence.

title: JABU alumni condemn INEC chair harassment in UK
description:
The President of the Joseph Ayo Babalola University Alumni Association, Akinkunmi Akintayo, has condemned the harassment and public intimidation of the Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Professor Joash Amupitan (SAN), during his recent visit to London, United Kingdom.
Akinta
content:
The President of the Joseph Ayo Babalola University Alumni Association, Akinkunmi Akintayo, has condemned the harassment and public intimidation of the Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Professor Joash Amupitan (SAN), during his recent visit to London, United Kingdom.
Akintayo described the incident, in which protesters reportedly surrounded the vehicle conveying the INEC chairman outside Chatham House and hurled insults at him, as an unfortunate development that falls short of the standards of civility and responsible public engagement expected in a democratic society.
Protesters targeted the INEC chairman on Thursday in London, where he went to deliver an address on Nigeria’s 2027 general elections and democratic trajectory at Chatham House, hosted in partnership with the Kimpact Development Initiative.
He stressed that while Nigerians have every right to question public institutions, demand accountability and express concerns about the electoral process, such engagements should be conducted through lawful, constructive and respectful channels rather than personal harassment or intimidation.
Akintayo emphasised the importance of protecting the dignity of public officeholders and preserving the institutional integrity of organisations entrusted with critical national responsibilities.
He noted that Amupitan’s position as INEC chairman comes with enormous national responsibility, particularly as Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections. Consequently, he urged Nigerians to allow the electoral body to discharge its constitutional responsibilities without unnecessary intimidation, while continuing to hold it accountable through legitimate democratic processes.
Akintayo’s intervention also reflects a longstanding institutional relationship between Amupitan and JABU.
Before he was appointed INEC chairman in October 2025, Amupitan served as the Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of the Governing Council of JABU, where he contributed to the university’s governance and administration.
A Nigerian based in the United Kingdom and a member of Chatham House, Tunmise Ajiboye, also condemned protesters’ harassment of the INEC chair.
In a statement on Saturday, Ajiboye called on United Kingdom authorities to investigate the incident thoroughly and ensure that anyone involved in the dastardly act is held accountable under the law.
He explained that Chatham House remained one of the world’s most respected platforms for policy dialogue, international affairs and democratic engagement.
He expressed deep disappointment that such a prestigious event was marred by an ambush outside the venue and near the UK Parliament area.
The Convener of Arewa Think Tank, Muhammad Alhaji Yakubu, also frowned on the alleged harassment of Amupitan.
He described the incident as a plot by disgruntled politicians to undermine Nigeria’s democracy ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Yakubu noted that those allegedly threatening to truncate the 2027 elections through sponsored protests, intimidation, and political blackmail would fail.
According to him, Nigerians would not allow the country’s democratic process to be sacrificed to selfish political interests.

title: Alabi retains Lagos Women Run title
description:
Aminat Alabi successfully defended her title at the 11th edition of the Lagos Women Run, winning the 10km race in 38 minutes, 37.26 seconds on Saturday.
Alabi, who became the first Lagos-based athlete to win the competition last year, finished ahead of Cameroonian Nguesta Lilian, who clocked 39:31.6
content:
Aminat Alabi successfully defended her title at the 11th edition of the Lagos Women Run, winning the 10km race in 38 minutes, 37.26 seconds on Saturday.

Alabi, who became the first Lagos-based athlete to win the competition last year, finished ahead of Cameroonian Nguesta Lilian, who clocked 39:31.68, while Jecinta Elias placed third in 40:32.12.

Thousands of women participated in the annual event, which started at Tafawa Balewa Square and ended at the Mobolaji Johnson Arena, Onikan.

Held under the theme, ‘One City, One Stride, Let’s Run Together’, the race promotes women’s participation in sports, fitness and healthy living.

Director-General of the Lagos State Sports Commission, Lekan Fatodu, praised the turnout and reaffirmed the state government’s support for the initiative.

“This is an exceptional run again, the turnout was impressive and the responses are inspiring.

“We are sending messages of wellness and the need for people to engage in a healthy lifestyle.

“Lagos State Government through the Lagos State Sports Commission will be available to continue to support. It’s a platform to promote inclusivity, so we will continue to promote and position them,” Fatodu said.

Beyond the race, the 11th edition featured a three-day empowerment programme held from November 10 to 12 at the Teslim Balogun Stadium, Surulere.

Organised by the Mateen Lander Impact Foundation, the programme focused on financial inclusion, business development, climate literacy and waste-to-wealth initiatives.

Participants received training on recycling, producing tyre ottoman stools and turning discarded materials into useful products, alongside sessions on health, hygiene, nutrition and wellness.

Executive Director of the foundation, Sidikat Folami, said the initiative was designed to help women identify economic opportunities within their communities, while race coordinator Tayo Popoola stressed that the event aimed to provide opportunities beyond the 10km competition through training and networking.

The post Alabi retains Lagos Women Run title appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Daga withdraws from Olympic Eagles squad
description:
Midfielder Daniel Daga has withdrawn from Nigeria’s Olympic Eagles squad after Norwegian club Molde reached an agreement with the Nigeria Football Federation to have him released.
Daga started in the 2-0 defeat to DR Congo in the first leg of the U23 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying tie in Lubumbash
content:
Midfielder Daniel Daga has withdrawn from Nigeria’s Olympic Eagles squad after Norwegian club Molde reached an agreement with the Nigeria Football Federation to have him released.

Daga started in the 2-0 defeat to DR Congo in the first leg of the U23 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying tie in Lubumbashi on Friday, and was booked in the 70th minute. He will now miss the return leg in Ikenne on Tuesday, November 17.

Injured Brighton and Hove Albion forward, Zadok Yohanna, who did not travel back to Lagos with the team, has also been allowed to return to his club.

Molde want Daga back for Friday’s Eliteserien game against Bodø/Glimt, last season’s UEFA Champions League surprise package, at the Aker Stadium.

The match is crucial for Molde, who are battling Lillestrøm, Rosenborg and Tromsø for a place in European competition with four matches left in the 2026 season.

The former Flying Eagles star has become one of the first names on manager Sindre Tjelmeland’s team sheet. He missed the club’s first 12 matches of the campaign because of off-field issues, but has since started 12 of Molde’s 14 league games.

He has also contributed in front of goal. Daga scored in consecutive matches against KFUM Oslo and Sarpsborg 08, and provided an assist against Lillestrøm last month.

title: We demand impeccable voter register
description: The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, must urgently clean up its battered image by producing an impeccable voters’ register ahead of the 2027 general elections. The discovery that its own officials allegedly compromised the database through fraudulent registrations is a monumental emb
content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, must urgently clean up its battered image by producing an impeccable voters’ register ahead of the 2027 general elections. The discovery that its own officials allegedly compromised the database through fraudulent registrations is a monumental embarrassment. It reinforces existing suspicions about the commission’s impartiality and competence at a time Nigerians desperately need an electoral umpire they can trust.

The scale of the problem is alarming. Of the more than 11 million people registered during the 2026 Continuous Voter Registration, CVR, exercise, INEC’s Automated Biometric Identification System, ABIS, flagged approximately 1.5 million entries as suspicious. The commission subsequently removed 1,277,252 invalid records, leaving about 268,000 requiring further verification. The preliminary national register contains over 103.4 million voters.

More disturbing is the alleged complicity of registration officers who abused their official login credentials to introduce fictitious identities. They reportedly uploaded AI-generated photographs, reused identical images and exploited registration provisions for persons with disabilities, claiming fictitious applicants had no fingers and could therefore bypass normal fingerprint verification. ABIS detected suspicious facial and biometric inconsistencies during screening.

Artificial intelligence has consequently introduced a dangerous dimension toa electoral fraud. Its capacity to generate convincing human faces makes fabricating identities easier and visual inspection less reliable. Although digitally enhanced photographs of genuine applicants are not necessarily fraudulent, fictitious identities must be identified and eliminated.

INEC says it has withdrawn implicated officers’ access credentials, commenced investigations, subjected suspicious entries to human adjudication and referred evidence for possible disciplinary action and prosecution. It promises further verification before the final register is displayed on December 15, 2026. These assurances are insufficient without demonstrable accountability. Public confidence in INEC was already fragile before this scandal.

Controversies surrounding previous elections, particularly the disputed 2023 presidential election and the failure of IReV to upload results as expected, have deepened distrust. A manipulated register could facilitate fictitious voting identities, impersonation, inflated constituency figures and deliberate disenfranchisement of legitimate voters. Biometric accreditation may prevent some abuses, but cannot excuse a defective database.

Professor JoashAmupitan must therefore open the corrective process to independent scrutiny. INEC should partner with opposition parties, civil society organisations, professional technology experts, the media and credible international electoral partners in conducting an independent forensic audit. The commission should publish state-by-state findings, preserve electronic evidence, identify and prosecute culprits, provide accessible mechanisms for genuine voters to challenge wrongful deletions and demonstrate BVAS and IReV readiness through independently observed tests.

The December 15 deadline must be respected without sacrificing accuracy. Less than two months before the elections, Nigeria cannot afford administrative confusion that could undermine the transition to a new government. These elections belong to Nigerians, not incumbent governments or political parties.

We demand an impeccable register, credible elections and leadership genuinely mandated by the Nigerian people.

The post We demand impeccable voter register appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Enyimba slump deepens as Inter Lagos end winless run
description:
Enyimba’s struggles in the Nigeria Premier Football League continued on Sunday as their losing streak extended, while Inter Lagos finally ended their eight-game winless run with a victory over Abia Warriors.
The People’s Elephant suffered another setback against Ikorodu City, leaving the nine-time c
content:
Enyimba’s struggles in the Nigeria Premier Football League continued on Sunday as their losing streak extended, while Inter Lagos finally ended their eight-game winless run with a victory over Abia Warriors.

The People’s Elephant suffered another setback against Ikorodu City, leaving the nine-time champions with more questions to answer as they battle to move away from the relegation zone.

Enyimba went into the Matchday 13 fixture under pressure after losing 1-0 to Ranchers Bees in Minna last weekend. They had been 18th on 11 points before the encounter, having recorded three wins, two draws and seven defeats in their opening 12 matches.

At the Mobolaji Johnson Arena in Lagos, Inter Lagos secured their first league victory in eight games with a win over Abia Warriors, ending a difficult spell for the newly promoted side.

The result provides a much-needed lift for Inter, who had struggled for consistency since their only previous league victory, a 1-0 away win over Enyimba in September.

Meanwhile, Rangers maintained their position at the top of the table despite being held to a draw by Niger Tornadoes in Minna.

The defending champions went into the match with 24 points from 11 games and were looking to extend their advantage over their closest challengers.

Katsina United also strengthened their title ambitions, moving into second place after defeating Nasarawa United at the Muhammadu Dikko Stadium.

The results provided another twist in the race at the top, while Enyimba’s continued struggles leave the Aba giants facing an increasingly difficult campaign.

title: S’West APC youths name advisory council chair
description:

The APC South-West Youth Leader, Adesuyi Daramola, said the ini
content:
The All Progressives Congress South-West Youth Leadership has appointed investment banking expert Adeola Olowe as chairperson of its Advisory Council to strengthen mentorship, strategic guidance, and youth development across the region.
The APC South-West Youth Leader, Adesuyi Daramola, said the initiative was a strategic step towards engaging accomplished individuals whose experience and credibility could provide additional guidance to young people beyond the mentorship available within the party.
According to a statement by the Media and Publicity Director, Office of the APC South-West Youth Leader, Remilekun Oyelowo, made available in Ado Ekiti on Sunday, Daramola spoke during the presentation of a certificate of appointment to Olowe.

He said, “The advisory council will help strengthen youth representation, develop leadership capacity and promote the effective implementation of programmes addressing the needs of young people across the South-West.”
According to the statement, Olowe is a finance professional with over 20 years of experience in investment banking and emerging financial markets.
It added that the appointment underscores the APC South-West Youth Leadership’s emphasis on mentorship, strategic engagement and leadership development as it seeks to strengthen youth participation and representation across the region.
Olowe, who thanked the APC South-West leadership for the appointment, described it as “an honour and a responsibility.”
The advisory council chair urged Nigerian youths “to believe in themselves, remain committed to hard work and contribute meaningfully to national development”.
While canvassing Nigerians’ continued support for the APC presidential candidate, President Bola Tinubu, in the January 16, 2027 election, Olowe described the president as a strategist whose record as Lagos State governor had shaped her confidence in his ability to plan for the country’s future.
The financial expert expressed support for the Tinubu administration’s economic reforms, saying the measures were intended to strengthen confidence in Nigeria’s economy.
She said, “I believe in Tinubu’s long-term vision, and I am confident in his approach to governance. Young Nigerians should remain committed to contributing to the country’s progress.”

title: ASUU Heroes Day, 2027 elections and the futuristic State Police, by Owei Lakemfa
description: It was one of the largest gatherings of Africa’s best brains. The date was November 12, the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) 2026 Heroes Day. The academics came from all parts of the country, gathering at the University of Abuja. Amongst them were current and former vice-chancellors, curr
content:
It was one of the largest gatherings of Africa’s best brains. The date was November 12, the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) 2026 Heroes Day. The academics came from all parts of the country, gathering at the University of Abuja. Amongst them were current and former vice-chancellors, current and past presidents of ASUU, and founding NLC President, Comrade Hassan Sunmonu. There was Alhaji Mahmud Yayale Ahmed, who has held three of the country’s highest public offices: Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Head of the Civil Service, and Minister of Defence. Former Bauchi State Governor AhmaduAdamuMu’azu, ex-Permanent Secretaries Professor GokeAdegoroye and Dr. TimiebiKoripamo-Agary, who, as serving Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Labour and Productivity, sued a Minister for conduct bordering on corruption.

Minister of State SuwaibaSa’idu Ahmad, a professor of Science Education, held herself up as a proud member of ASUU, identified the principle of good welfare for academics, and urged all to continuously help build bridges between Government and ASUU.

The occasion embodied three primary characteristics of the seventy-eight-year-old ASUU. First, ever analysing the past, which is why it annually marks its Heroes Day to honour those who have made sacrifices for the union, universities, and the country. The Day commemorates November 12, 2013, the date former ASUU President and noted novelist Festus Iyayi was killed in a car crash. He was travelling for an ASUU National Executive Council meeting in Kano to find a solution to a national strike triggered by Government’s intransigence and insistence on defunding education.

The second ASUU culture is ever interrogating the present, which is why this year’s theme focused on the electoral system. The third is the union’s tendency to probe into the future. This time, it looked at the ongoing attempts to create State Police and the possible impact it could have on the 2027 General Elections.

ASUU is also quite strategic in building alliances, which is why its awardees this year included a number of people who led the Government Negotiating Teams or played roles in ensuring the success of the decades-long ASUU-Government negotiations. These included Alhaji Ahmed, Professor MunzaliJibril, whose Negotiating Team in May 2021 broke through barriers and successfully produced a draft agreement, and Professor NimiDimkpa Briggs, who, on June 16, 2022, despite government reservations, followed through with a new draft agreement within ten weeks.

The Buhari government had been so displeased with the breakthrough the Briggs Team had made with ASUU that it made false accusations against the likeable professor. It accused him of excluding government agencies from the negotiations, inflating academics’ salaries by N1.1 trillion, and acting out of financial self-interest. In making the last two allegations, it escaped the government’s mind that Briggs had retired from service and, as such, would not be a beneficiary of the enhanced academics’ pay. When Briggs passed on ten months later, the same Buhari government praised him to high heavens for his dignity, truthfulness, and “historic contributions” to education.

Alhaji Ahmed, speaking on behalf of the awardees, joked about his experience with ASUU President Chris Piwuna, a professor of psychiatry whom he said tried to make him his patient, but he rejected such negotiation tactics. He dedicated his award to former ASUU President and current Trustee, Professor AsisiAsobie, whom he said introduced him to the union’s unique ways of negotiation. Asobie, he said, would refuse to even drink water in his office because they were negotiating.

Professor Piwuna, in analysing the situation in the country, said: “The Nigerian Universities and our members have suffered their share of violence and trauma. Some campuses were attacked; we have lost members across branches, and several students have been killed, staff displaced, and properties lost. Our universities have become theatres of ‘war’ and easy targets for insurgents, from Jos to Abuja, and campuses in North West Nigeria.”

I had the honour of delivering the 2026 ASUU Annual Lecture titled: ‘Insecurity, Incumbency and Elections in Nigeria: The Role of State Police.’

I pointed out that in the past eleven years of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) administrations of Buhari and Tinubu, at least 97,111 persons have been killed in violent conflicts. Also, that Nigeria, in the 2026 Global Terrorism Index (GTI) Report, ranks fourth globally, trailing Pakistan, Burkina Faso, and Niger.

I therefore submitted that even with the assistance of the military, the police are not coping with insecurity. I listed challenges of the police as including their inability to wean themselves of their colonial origins of relying on force, repression, and suppression of Nigerians rather than being a civil agency and a friend of the people. Other problems I mentioned are very poor remuneration and welfare and job insecurity, particularly amongst its top echelons. One of the suggestions I made was that, career-wise, the police should be run like the public service, where the promotion of a few as Permanent Secretaries or Head of Service does not mean all the Directors senior to them are sacked. In the alternative, that a non-policeman, such as a judge or senior lawyer, be made the Inspector General of Police (IGP). If a non-soldier can be the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, a non-policeman can be the IGP.

These challenges, I posited, make the establishment of State Police necessary, especially when they will be recruited from locals familiar with the terrain and local culture. The fact that there will be multiple police agencies would not lead to administrative challenges, as the United States runs 17,985 police agencies and Canada, 160. The challenges I see include whether state governments that cannot pay workers’ salaries can afford State Police or whether governors who employ thugs would not recruit them into the State Police.

Again, can state governors that would not allow their State Electoral Commissions or Local Governments to run properly allow professionalism in their State Police?

Our politics itself, I submitted, is being transformed into a criminal enterprise in which true primaries are hardly held, opposition supporters are beaten and prevented from casting their ballots or threatened with death, and results are written sometimes before elections. I submitted that elections in the country, which should be as simple as the holder of the National Identity Card voting at any polling unit and their vote being automatically transmitted to central and local collation centres, have been made unnecessarily cumbersome with voter cards, ballot papers, card readers, BVAS, IREV, collation centres, etcetera.

My conclusion is that, with the Presidential Elections nine weeks away, it is unlikely the State Police will be in place before then. Even if it is, with 32 governors siding with the ruling party and an unreformed police, no fundamental changes to the usual partisan policing will take place

The post ASUU Heroes Day, 2027 elections and the futuristic State Police, by Owei Lakemfa appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Nigeria: One-party or one-man state? By Suleiman A. Suleiman
description:
Since at least late 2024, when President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had been in office for barely 18 months, politicians and other Nigerians have been saying that the country is drifting into a one-party state. These warnings have not only grown louder in recent months; they are justified.



The All Progres
content:
Since at least late 2024, when President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had been in office for barely 18 months, politicians and other Nigerians have been saying that the country is drifting into a one-party state. These warnings have not only grown louder in recent months; they are justified.

The All Progressives Congress (APC) now controls 31 out of 36 states, since at least the middle of this year, when the 2027 election campaigns entered top gear. At the end of the 2023 election cycle, the APC controlled 21 states, including the off-cycle election in Edo State in 2024. This means that, in the last year, 10 sitting governors have defected from their original parties to join Tinubu in the APC. The reverse traffic, meanwhile, is zero. This is unlike the 2015 election cycle, when leading politicians were defecting from the then ruling People’s Democratic Party (PDP) to the then main opposition APC.

At the same time, the transformation of political organisation and opposition parties that we witnessed during 2013–2015 does not appear to be happening this time, as the leading opposition parties remain ridden by crippling crises that President Tinubu and the APC have been accused of instigating. First of all, the PDP is now a one-man show, and it is difficult to even know what the party stands for or who its leading members are, other than FCT Minister Nyesom Wike. More significantly, in 2023, the Labour Party (LP) and the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP) won 63 seats between them—almost all of them for the first time in history—in the National Assembly elections, and a total of 12 states and the FCT in the presidential election by their candidates, Mr Peter Obi and Dr Rabiu Kwankwaso, combined.

That was a formidable performance, particularly by Peter Obi, but both the LP and the NNPP are no longer serious contenders in this election, and the two men have since left to meet on the same presidential ticket in the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC). Accusing fingers also point to Tinubu for making their own political parties unviable platforms for the two men. This leaves the African Democratic Congress (ADC), which faces the most crisis of all. For almost a year, the ADC, formed by a partial coalition of like-minded and opposition interests, has been held hostage by the antics of one man, enabled almost entirely by Nigerian courts.

The status of ADC candidates, from the presidential to the state assembly elections, currently hangs in limbo because Nigerian courts in this era now think that the dubious concerns of one party member are more important than the will of all the voters in the hundreds of primary elections conducted by the APC in the past months.

In short, Nigeria today looks like a one-party state, with the ruling APC as the last man standing. In my view, however, Nigeria is not sliding into a one-party state. It is already a one-man state.

A one-party state—a country where a single political party dominates the political space—is a form of authoritarian rule, whether codified in law or in practical effect. In practice, however, there can be significant checks, political pressure and opposition within the ruling one party itself. More importantly, while undemocratic, one-party states tend to be developmental. They typically maintain political legitimacy through rapid industrialisation and all-round national development, as illustrated by the former Communist countries in Europe, including the defunct USSR, and most strikingly by today’s Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which lifted more than 600 million people out of acute poverty in under 30 years.

Tinubu’s APC is nothing like a one-party state in this sense because the twin scaffolds of legitimacy—a serious national development agenda and internal checks—are wholly lacking. Instead, we have a president who straddles his party and the nation without any effective guardrails to his power. That is not a one-party state; it is, rather, a one-man state, whereby nearly all formal institutions of the state, all political parties, civil society, and other informal power brokers no longer provide any meaningful constraints on the will of the president. That is not good for Nigeria, and I am not sure it is something good for the President himself.

Since 1999, Nigeria has never really had a true multi-party or two-party system, with the exception of the two-year period between 2013 and 2015. What we have always had is a pseudo-one-party state, whereby a single political party dominates the political space: first the PDP, from 1999 to 2013, and then the APC, during 2015–2023. But even during those years of pseudo-democracy, there were at least two important guardrails against presidential power that ensured that our democracy continued to grow and thrive.

First, ruling party politics in Nigeria since 1999 was always characterised by significant political pressure and opposition within the party itself, even in the near absence of an effectively coordinated or strong opposition party. That pressure and opposition came from various factions of the ruling party, or from other centres of power within the party and government. Secondly, there was significant and effective opposition from outside the party and government, particularly from the media, labour unions and organised civil society.

The result was that no president was able to win or get everything he wanted all the time. For example, former President Olusegun Obasanjo was the most powerful of Nigerian leaders from 1999 to 2023. But even at the peak of his power, Obasanjo still faced serious pressure and opposition from ruling party chairs, governors, members and leaders of the National Assembly, etc., many of whom frequently disagreed or clashed openly with him. Industrial strikes by unions were effective enough to compel the government to backtrack on some of its policies. Newspapers and civil society organisations were firm and stringent in their criticisms of presidential overreach. It was only natural, then, that Obasanjo’s third-term bid was defeated.

Presidents Umar Yar’Adua, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari were all more or less the same, as significant power blocks within and outside the ruling party and government provided significant checks on their power. The Governors’ Forum was a powerful wedge on Yar’Adua, and, since 1999, the National Assembly was probably most assertive under Buhari’s first term. Governors Uzo Kalu of Abia and Attahiru Bafarawa of Sokoto fought tooth and nail against Obasanjo, not to mention Senate President Chuba Okadigbo, Speaker Ghali Na’Abba and even Dimeji Bankole, just as Governor Ortom screamed at Buhari daily for eight years.

If for nothing else, these pressures were useful for defeating Obasanjo’s “third term”, for getting Yar’Adua to initiate enduring reforms in our electoral system, for the doctrine of necessity that made Jonathan President, for forcing Jonathan to accept defeat in the 2015 elections, and for making a democrat out of Buhari—all of which, and more, are important moments of progress in our democratic journey. But my broader point is that all of these guardrails of our developing democracy have been blown off, bought up or buried under the rubble of President Tinubu’s silent corrosion of Nigerian politics, economy and society, leaving us with something worse than a pseudo-one-party state: that is, a one-man state.

The ruling APC itself, the National Assembly, the governors, including those pretending to belong to other parties, the courts, the anti-corruption agencies, large sections of the religious and traditional establishment, and equally large sections of the media and so-called “civil society” all appear to be answering to or doing the bidding of one man in Nigeria today. Only Nigerians and their date with INEC in January and February are now left standing. We will see.

This article was previously published 11 months ago, but has been updated to reflect current events.

The post Nigeria: One-party or one-man state? By Suleiman A. Suleiman appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: PenCom opens up on N52,000 minimum pension guarantee
description:
By Victor Ahiuma-Young



The National Pension Commission, PenCom, has shed light on the implementation of the long-awaited Minimum Pension Guarantee, MPG, disclosing that 173,209 Nigerian retirees are eligible to benefit from a guaranteed minimum monthly pension of N52,500 following its formal acti
content:
By Victor Ahiuma-Young

The National Pension Commission, PenCom, has shed light on the implementation of the long-awaited Minimum Pension Guarantee, MPG, disclosing that 173,209 Nigerian retirees are eligible to benefit from a guaranteed minimum monthly pension of N52,500 following its formal activation by President Bola Tinubu.

The initiative, aimed at improving the welfare and financial security of retirees under the Contributory Pension Scheme, CPS, was unveiled alongside a healthcare programme designed to provide free access to essential medical services for low-income pensioners.

The two initiatives, the Minimum Pension Guarantee and the Pension Industry Healthcare Plan (PenCare), were announced at the Presidential Pension Security Initiatives ceremony held at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja.

Tinubu, who was represented at the event by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, said the Minimum Pension Guarantee fulfilled a provision of the Pension Reform Act 2004, which was retained in the 2014 legislation but had remained unimplemented for 22 years.

Declaring the scheme operational, the President assured pension contributors that the government would no longer allow eligible retirees to receive pensions below the guaranteed minimum threshold. “From this day, there is a floor beneath the Nigerian retiree. No one who contributed under the Contributory Pension Scheme will ever be allowed to fall below,” he said.

The President urged successive administrations to sustain the policy and periodically increase the guaranteed amount rather than discontinue it.

On the healthcare component, President Tinubu said the Pension Industry Healthcare Plan, PenCare, was designed to shield vulnerable retirees from medical expenses that could deplete their retirement savings.

He said beneficiaries would receive healthcare access cards in the coming months, enabling them to access essential medical services without bearing the financial burden.

The President also disclosed that his administration had issued a N758 billion bond to address outstanding pension arrears and approved a N32,000 monthly consequential adjustment for affected federal pensioners.

He added that state governments had collectively spent more than N1 trillion settling outstanding pension obligationsSpeaking at the ceremony, PenCom Director-General, Omolola Oloworaran, disclosed that 173,209 retirees had qualified for the N52,500 monthly minimum pension.

She explained that the beneficiaries comprised 34 per cent of retirees from federal service, 12 per cent from state employment and 54 per cent from the private sector.

According to her, the guaranteed amount was determined through actuarial validation and would be reviewed periodically to ensure its sustainability.

Oloworaran further disclosed that “more than N400 billion is s available in the Pension Protection Fund to support the implementation of the initiative.”

She noted that over 65 per cent of private-sector retirees currently received monthly pensions below the newly established threshold, underscoring the importance of the intervention.

Providing further details, Oloworaran said the pension industry had committed “more than N7 billion to the programme, with insurance premiums already paid to provide healthcare coverage for nearly 30,000 retirees.”

Meanwhile, Chairman of Heirs Holdings, Mr Tony Elumelu, described the initiatives as investments in human dignity, pledging private-sector support for efforts aimed at strengthening retirement security and promoting financial inclusion.

Speaking at the event, Elumelu particularly praised the pension industry for funding PenCare, calling it “a powerful demonstration of what responsible institutions can achieve when they put people first.”

He assured that “the private sector stands ready to support policies and partnerships that strengthen our institutions.”

Framing the programmes within his “Africapitalism” philosophy, which holds that economic growth must “translate into improved lives”, Elumelu added: “I congratulate Mr. President, the leadership of PenCom led by Omolara Oloworaran, and all stakeholders who have made today’s milestone possible.”

title: Tinubu, 2027 and the price of losing trusted journalism
description:
By SEGUN ADEDIRAN



In London last week, Sarah Lester, editor of the Manchester Evening News, stood before Parliament to open this year’s Journalism Matters campaign. She was not pleading for sympathy. She was asking a question that every democracy must now answer.



The British prime minister had
content:
By SEGUN ADEDIRAN

In London last week, Sarah Lester, editor of the Manchester Evening News, stood before Parliament to open this year’s Journalism Matters campaign. She was not pleading for sympathy. She was asking a question that every democracy must now answer.

The British prime minister had promised that “trusted local journalism remains at the heart of communities.” Lester wanted to know what that promise actually meant. How far, she asked, is power willing to go to ensure that journalism does not merely survive, but thrives?

It was a British speech, delivered to a British audience, about a British crisis. Yet in the Nigerian media industry, it landed with an uncomfortable familiarity. For Nigeria is facing the same question, only more urgently, and with far higher stakes.

We are heading toward 2027. Another general election is approaching. And the institutions that are supposed to make that election legible — the newspapers, the local radio stations, the investigative newsrooms that have held Nigerian democracy together since 1999 — are bleeding out.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu knows this world intimately. He is not a stranger to the press. He is a media proprietor. He was a central figure in the pro-democracy struggle of the 1990s, when independent newspapers were not a luxury but a weapon — printed in secret, distributed at great risk, read as acts of defiance against military rule. He understands, perhaps better than any president before him, that without a free press, there is no democratic contest. There is only noise.

In March, when he met with media leaders, the president spoke well. He acknowledged the plight of the press. He promised support. Those words mattered. But promises do not pay for newsprint. They do not keep a bureau in Sokoto open. They do not stop a young reporter from leaving journalism for public relations because journalism can no longer pay rent.

That is the question now before the Villa: What will this administration actually do?

The crisis is not abstract. It is arithmetic.

Hyperinflation has made newsprint, ink, plates and broadcast equipment prohibitively expensive. The naira’s devaluation has turned what was once a difficult business into an impossible one. Advertising, once the lifeblood of newspapers, has migrated to platforms that did not create the journalism they profit from. Google and Meta extract enormous value from Nigerian reporting — our investigations, our headlines, our photographs — while returning almost nothing to the newsrooms that produced them.

At the same time, the information environment has become toxic. WhatsApp, TikTok and Facebook are flooded with doctored videos, invented endorsements and AI-generated falsehoods. In an election year, that flood becomes a weapon. When professional newsrooms shrink, misinformation does not merely fill the vacuum. It becomes the vacuum.

This is not a sentimental argument for nostalgia. It is a structural argument for democracy.

Elections require a shared factual basis. Voters need to know what candidates promised, what governments delivered, what budgets contained, what courts decided. Without trusted local journalism, there is no reliable record. Without a reliable record, accountability collapses. And where accountability collapses, corruption and violence flourish.

The world is no longer debating whether to act. It is acting.

On Nov. 11, the European Commission formally presented its proposed Digital Fairness Act, aimed at manipulative “dark patterns,” addictive design features like autoplay and infinite scroll, and deceptive influencer marketing. Violators could face fines of up to 6 per cent of global turnover. It recognises that platforms cannot be left to regulate themselves.

In Britain, the Competition and Markets Authority has opened an investigation into Meta over new content terms that would allow the company to use publisher content to train its artificial intelligence systems — without fair compensation. The question is no longer whether AI will be built on journalism. It is whether journalism will be paid for it.

In the United States, after Democrats swept both chambers in the midterms, incoming lawmakers have signalled hearings with tech chief executives and federal AI oversight legislation. Even President Donald Trump, long resistant to regulation, has said he is open to working with Democrats on AI guardrails — provided they do not cause American innovation to fall behind China’s.

And in Africa, the stakes are becoming visible in stark relief. On Nov. 11, after a 248-day suspension, Gabon restored access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube — but under new ordinances regulating AI-generated content, requiring personal identification, and establishing direct moderation agreements between the state regulator and the platforms. It is a blunt, imperfect model, but it reflects a continental realisation: unregulated platforms are a threat to sovereignty itself.

Nigeria cannot afford to watch this global reordering from the sidelines. Supporting journalism does not mean subsidising sycophancy. It does not mean creating a state press. It means treating independent news as what it is: public-interest infrastructure, as essential as roads and courts.

The challenges of elections and campaigns can be daunting. But the President will etch his name in media history if he’s able to fix this digital anomie in record time. A press that is starved into dependence is no more free than a press that is censored into silence.

There is a particular irony here. President Tinubu rose to power through a political movement that depended on a fearless press to survive. The newspapers that carried the June 12 struggle, that exposed military excesses, that kept the idea of democracy alive when democracy was illegal — those papers did not survive because they were profitable. They survived because Nigerians believed journalism was worth dying for.

Today, journalism is not asking Nigerians to die for it. It is asking the state to stop letting it die of neglect.

As we approach 2027, the choice is stark. We can enter the election with a weakened, impoverished press, overwhelmed by AI-generated propaganda and platform-driven misinformation — an election where no one trusts anything, and therefore no one trusts the result. Or we can enter it with a renewed, financially viable, independent press capable of informing voters, checking power and telling the Nigerian story truthfully.

Lester warned Britain not to take journalism for granted “even for a second.” Nigeria has taken it for granted for far too long.

President Tinubu has a historic opportunity — not merely to praise the press, as he did in March, but to save it. That would be his most enduring democratic legacy. Not a road, not a refinery, but a republic where truth still has a home.

The time to act is not after 2027. It is now, before the light dims further.

•Adediran is the Chief Executive Officer of the Newspaper Proprietors’ Association of Nigeria

The post Tinubu, 2027 and the price of losing trusted journalism appeared first on Vanguard News.

The message, signed by the Force Secretar
content:
The Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, has ordered the posting of 13 Assistant Inspectors-General of Police and two Commissioners of Police to new commands and departments across the country, according to a police wireless message dated November 15.

The message, signed by the Force Secretariat in Abuja and addressed to all zonal, state and specialised commands, said the postings take effect immediately and were marked “most immediate.”

Enyinnaya I. Adiogu was posted as AIG in charge of Zone 4, Makurdi, while Ibrahim Maikaba Balarabe was sent to Zone 7, Abuja. Ohagwu Felix Ndukwe was posted to Zone 17, Akure, and Regina Cosmas Udoette to Zone 16, Yenagoa.

At Force Headquarters, Clement Robert was named AIG in charge of the Force Criminal Investigation Department (FCID), while Olusegun Eyitayo Omosayin heads the Department of Training and Development.

Afolabi Wilfred Olutokunbo moves to the Department of Operations (DOPS), Martin O. Nwogoh to the Police Air Wing, and Ibrahim Gotan to the Force Intelligence Department (FID).

Other AIGs were posted to commands outside the headquarters. Betty Enekpen Otimeyin goes to the Maritime Command in Lagos, Ugobueze Ogbodo to the FCID Annex in Enugu, Taylor Lennox Olarenwaju to the Coordination (COOP) office in Lagos, and Shetima Jauro Mohammed to the Border Patrol Force (BPF) in Abuja.

“The Force Secretariat, Nigeria Police Force, Abuja, on behalf of the Inspector-General of Police, announces the posting of senior officers as follows, with immediate effect.

“The Inspector-General of Police has ordered the posting of the following Assistant Inspectors-General of Police:

AIG Enyinnaya I. Adiogu, fsi, to Zone 4, Makurdi, as AIG. AIG Clement Robert, fsi, to the Force Criminal Investigation Department, Force Headquarters, Abuja, as AIG.

AIG Betty Enekpen Otimeyin, to the Maritime Command, Lagos.

AIG Ibrahim Maikaba Balarabe to Zone 7, Abuja, as AIG. AIG Olusegun Eyitayo Omosayin, fdc, to the Department of Training and Development, Force Headquarters, Abuja, as AIG.

“AIG Ugobueze Ogbodo to the FCID Annex, Enugu, as AIG.

AIG Ohagwu Felix Ndukwe to Zone 17, Akure, as AIG.

AIG Taylor Lennox Olarenwaju to the Coordination (COOP) office, Lagos, as AIG. AIG Regina Cosmas Udoette to Zone 16, Yenagoa, as AIG. AIG Afolabi Wilfred Olutokunbo to the Department of Operations, Force Headquarters, Abuja, as AIG.

“AIG Martin O. Nwogoh to the Air Wing, Force Headquarters, Abuja, as AIG. AIG Shetima Jauro Mohammed to the BPF, Abuja, as AIG. AIG Ibrahim Gotan to the Force Intelligence Department, Abuja, as AIG,” the wireless message read.

Two CPs who were posted on higher-duty assignments also got new roles.

Gabriel Onyilo Elaigwu was named AIG in charge of Armament at the Department of Operations, Force Headquarters, while Abbas Sule became AIG in charge of Interpol in Abuja.

On the matter of rank, the message said the two commissioners should not wear the AIG rank while on higher duty. In the words of the message, “Officers on higher duty post should not wear the rank.”

The Force Secretariat also directed that the postings be handled by the Computer, Establishment and Records units, and instructed commands to update their records accordingly.

The post Police shake-up: IG redeploys 15 AIGs, CPs appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
