title: Development challenges in Delta: Ebitonmo’s theory of political thermodynamics
description:
By Enewaridideke Ekanpou



Alapala Anthony Ebitonmo, the man currently representing Burutu North Constituency in the Delta State House of Assembly, is again furious, as it is his wont to be, resistant to every benevolent arrester unleashed on him. Rather retrospectively, in a blazing fury, he was r
content:
By Enewaridideke Ekanpou

Alapala Anthony Ebitonmo, the man currently representing Burutu North Constituency in the Delta State House of Assembly, is again furious, as it is his wont to be, resistant to every benevolent arrester unleashed on him. Rather retrospectively, in a blazing fury, he was recently sighted at Oyangbene and approvingly led into the open arms of people carrying “chalked hearts.” The hearts of Oyangbene people became immediately “chalked” because Ebitonmo was suddenly sighted. Even in their variedly chalked hearts at the sight of the man, they were confounded, thrown off balance, when they were told he had not come for Oyangbene community. Even in their confoundment, they sought to know the rationale behind Ebitonmo’s sudden appearance in Oyangbene when he claimed openly he had not come for the Oyangbene community. In a characteristic blazing fury, he was curtly categorical that his sudden appearance was rooted in two propellants—Serikoromo Primary School and his famed theory named political thermodynamics.

Available statistics reveal Serikoromo Primary School in Burutu Local Government Area of Delta State had been the home of rickety structures for decades, daily rendezvoused by pythons, leopards, elephants, lions, grasscutters, lizards, iguanas, rats, cats, and bats. To teachers and pupils, these reptiles and mammals became the bandits troubling them. For decades, they cried their eyes out with tears that spread like the waters of the Atlantic Ocean. However, their impassioned tears looked like the silvery waters in the ocean; they were not comforted like the weeping Biblical Martha. Serikoromo Primary School, founded in 1956, was where I had my primary education in 1988. The oceanic tears of this school had known many decades of neglect.

Awakened to the pathetic story of Serikoromo Primary School, Ebitonmo became blazingly furious. With a blazing fury that carried the troubling pains of the poor teachers and pupils, Ebitonmo risked a sudden flight to Serikoromo Primary School without a visible speedboat professionally skimming the white waters of Oyangbene River. His presence in the school was equivalent to ritualistically stepping on “Atu” in a folktale stunningly told by TimiebiMaika. Mystically, as captured in Timiebi’s folktales, ritualistically stepping on the “Atu” was imbued with the power to make one appear dramatically at the backyard of one’s house. The power of invisibility and disappearance dwells mystically in the “Atu” ritual. The second propellant of Ebitonmo’s appearance in Oyangbene without a visible flight was his treasured philosophy of political thermodynamics.

Political thermodynamics is the measurable degree of responsiveness of, or applicability of, core developmental ideas to visible development challenges that plague communities and mankind in general. It is the space for the transformation of strategically formulated developmental ideas into enduring visible structures through the interrogative interaction between formulated developmental ideas and the real challenges of development that trouble mankind in different dimensions of life. It is a pragmatic interrogative interface aimed at the delivery of visible, measurable structures of development. Political thermodynamics also centres on creating a measurable merger between electoral promises and visible structures—visible structures viewed as emanations from the electoral promises upon which the representational mandate of Ebitonmo stands.

Ebitonmo thinks endlessly in development terms for both biotic and abiotic factors in Burutu North Constituency. For Ebitonmo, Serikoromo Primary School was another experimentation ground for a measurable test of his theory of political thermodynamics underlying all his political and representational conversations, interactions, and engagements as a singular ideational propelling force. At work, political thermodynamics shows how Ebitonmo’s ideational formulations flow and confront core development challenges of the people, transforming them in pragmatic terms into visible and measurable structures, in demonstration of the dominance of his developmental formulations over visible development challenges. In Ebitonmo, the merger between theoretical formulations and pragmatic delivery is demonstrably visible. This is what Ebitonmo has just demonstrated at Serikoromo Primary School in Oyangbene.

Ebitonmo’s journey to Oyangbene is driven by his blazing fury that my primary school is abandoned, and this abandonment has consumed many years. He is also driven by his political thermodynamics theory, or his prized philosophy of representation. This theory centres on how his humanistic political ideas interact with core development challenges of the people at the grassroots level. His humanistic ideals merge into the developmental challenges of the people to transform lives measured in infrastructure. His ideas confront the development problems, solve them, and transform the people. His theory is a measure of how humanistic ideas transform lives through interaction with and confrontation of their core developmental problems. Every community touched by him is a reflection of how his philosophy of political thermodynamics bulldozes and transforms communities through visible projects executed. In every move, Ebitonmo is guided by his famed political thermodynamics philosophy—a political philosophy his political opponents cannot match strength for strength and idea for idea.

Pragmatic and indestructible, political thermodynamics is inspiring and striking in its theoretical composition and applicability.

Though an inspiring and striking political theory it is, it must be admitted that thermodynamics, from which Ebitonmo’s political thermodynamics is derived, was foundationally erected and came into being through the scientific exertions of multiple scientists in the 19th century, like Rudolf Clausius, James Watt, William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), Walter Nernst, and others. However, among the multiple scientific exertions which gave birth to thermodynamics, Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot was widely acclaimed as the father of thermodynamics based on his successful publication on thermodynamics in 1824.

The decades-old governmental neglect of Serikoromo Primary School has just been ended by Ebitonmo through his phenomenal display of blazing fury on flight to Oyangbene without a visible flight. In Serikoromo Primary School, an architecturally arresting block of four classrooms now bestrides the compound like an angelic creature on a visit of no return to the school. Pride has been restored to the school where I had my primary education. I can now proudly “pound” my chest and proclaim ubiquitously that I was the senior prefect of Serikoromo Primary School in 1988. No special sermon or discourse is further required to attest to the viability of Ebitonmo’s theoretical formulations encapsulated in his philosophy of political thermodynamics. Either for a visible block of classrooms or visible desks and tables for teachers and pupils, Ebitonmo’s developmentally audacious philosophy of political thermodynamics has been felt in Okpokunou, Edegbene, Enekorogha, Bikorogha, Gbekebor, Obotebe, Ayakoromo, Gbekebor, Kiagbodo, Opuapale, Labolouseigha, and Bubougbene in Burutu North Constituency.

Representationally building a verifiable merger between theoretical formulations and pragmatic delivery is not an easy task, but Ebitonmo has just achieved it without a flourish. This is commendable in every dimension. To pull off this representational feat, representational encore is the natural harvest, the stipend, the appreciatory recognition of this performance. The political thermodynamics theory of Ebitonmo is too viable and relevant to be ignored by this generation. The scaffolding needed for this viable political philosophy to thrive must be afforded a space. This means the people of Burutu Constituency must speak the unifying language of “bitter kola” in the 2027 general elections. The language of bitter kola spoken in the waiting 2027 general elections, we are sure of Ebitonmo’s developmentally blazing fury and his beloved philosophy of political thermodynamics, whose pragmatic power of developmental communication has been asserted in Serikoromo Primary School. Historically, Ebitonmo has become the fearless arrester of dilapidated structures in Serikoromo Primary School, Oyangbene. A referentially bold and furious arrester Ebitonmo has become, steadily reinforced and sustained in every step by Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s MORE agenda.

*Dr. Ekanpou writes from Akparenogbene, Delta State.

The post Development challenges in Delta: Ebitonmo’s theory of political thermodynamics appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: 2027: I’m running to win, vows Makinde
description:
Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, has declared that he will seek only a four-year presidential term if elected in 2027, arguing that Southern Nigeria should complete its eight-year turn in the presidency by 2031.
Makinde, who is contesting the presidential ticket on the platform of Allied People’s M
content:
Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, has declared that he will seek only a four-year presidential term if elected in 2027, arguing that Southern Nigeria should complete its eight-year turn in the presidency by 2031.

Makinde, who is contesting the presidential ticket on the platform of Allied People’s Movement, said he was entering the contest to win and would not seek a second term, linking his position to what he described as fairness, national unity and respect for the country’s political understanding on power rotation.

The governor also said his proposed administration would prioritise security, employment, enterprise development and stronger public institutions under his Reset Agenda.

His campaign office, in a statement on Sunday, said Makinde believed the South should be allowed to complete the remaining four years of its eight-year presidential tenure before power returned to the North in 2031.

“His commitment to a single four-year term is rooted in his belief that national unity rests on fairness, mutual respect and fidelity to the understandings that hold our federation together.

“Southern Nigeria should complete its remaining four years in the presidency, bringing its turn to eight years by 2031,” the statement said.

The governor’s position makes a one-term presidency a central part of his pitch to Nigerians as political manoeuvring intensifies ahead of the next general election.

The campaign office said the proposed four years would be tied to specific governance priorities rather than an extended stay in office.

“Those four years must count in the lives of Nigerians. His priorities are to restore security, expand opportunities for enterprise and employment, strengthen public institutions and give families confidence in their future. He is seeking a mandate tied to clear priorities and measurable results,” it added.

The statement also said Makinde had been engaging political leaders and Nigerians across different social groups as part of efforts to build support for his presidential ambition.

It described the engagements as part of his attempt to secure the political backing required to win the election and govern effectively.

“Makinde is in this contest to earn the people’s trust, win their votes and serve as President for one purposeful four-year term,” the campaign office stated.

It added that his Reset Agenda would guide his campaign and that the governor was taking his message to citizens across the country.

title: PINL’s host community strategy and the future of oil pipeline security
description:
By Tayo Olu



Protecting oil pipelines in the Niger Delta requires more than the surveillance of facilities and the deployment of security personnel. The pipelines run through communities whose relationships with operators, access to economic opportunities and grievances over local development can
content:
By Tayo Olu

Protecting oil pipelines in the Niger Delta requires more than the surveillance of facilities and the deployment of security personnel. The pipelines run through communities whose relationships with operators, access to economic opportunities and grievances over local development can influence the security of the infrastructure.

This relationship between community participation and pipeline security was the focus of a recent study by Dr. Oyeinfie Emmanuel Jonjon, a sociologist at Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, Port Harcourt, who examined Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL)’s approach to pipeline surveillance along the Trans Niger Pipeline (TNP).

Jonjon, a lecturer and researcher in the Department of Sociology, Faculty of Social Sciences, at Ignatius Ajuru University of Education in Rumuolumeni, Port Harcourt, Rivers State, has developed what he calls the ‘Weaver Colony Theory of Communal Living,’ using PINL’s community-based surveillance model to examine how host communities, private security contractors and statutory agencies can work within a common framework.

His paper, published in August 2026 in the American Journal of Social and Humanitarian Research (Volume 7, Issue 8, pages 126 to 145), is titled “Community-Based Surveillance of Oil and Gas Pipeline Infrastructure in the Niger Delta: A Theoretical Analysis of Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited Through Structural Functionalism and Weaver Colony Theory.”

The study examines how host communities, surveillance firms and security agencies can share responsibilities in protecting oil pipelines while maintaining clearly defined roles.

Jonjon believes that the cooperation of host communities is as important as the security measures put in place to protect oil infrastructure, and oil companies must build lasting relationships with host communities if they want to protect their facilities.

Pipeline theft, illegal bunkering, vandalism and production disruptions have remained persistent problems in the Niger Delta. Jonjon argued that addressing them mainly through security operations overlooks the influence of host communities and their relationships with oil operators.

He argued that operators often turn to media campaigns or spending on host communities after security incidents, while their corporate social responsibility programmes have done little to resolve longstanding grievances.

The TNP, which passes through communities in Rivers, Imo and Abia states, provides the setting for his examination of PINL’s operations. PINL, which was incorporated in 2019 to provide engineering, construction and security services to the country’s oil and gas sector, uses community-based surveillance along the pipeline corridor.

Jonjon’s argument is based on Structural Functionalism, a sociological theory developed by thinkers such as Émile Durkheim, Talcott Parsons and Robert K. Merton. The theory explains how different parts of society have roles that contribute to the stability of the whole.

However, he argued that the theory does not fully account for power imbalances, historical grievances or disagreements over who has the right to speak for a community. It also offers little guidance on how private operators should involve residents in their day-to-day activities.

He used the Weaver Colony Theory to explain how different groups can work together while maintaining their individual roles. He described the idea as “Many Nests, One Tree,” which was borrowed from weaver-bird colonies.

The tree represents the shared physical, economic, social and institutional environment, while the nests represent the different groups operating within it. Each group has its own responsibilities but must work together for the system to function.

In the framework, host communities contribute local knowledge, continuous presence and vigilance. A surveillance firm like PINL provides professional monitoring, operational coordination and structured engagement. Statutory security agencies and regulators retain their legal authority, enforcement responsibilities and oversight functions under the Petroleum Industry Act.

The model encourages community participation in pipeline protection without giving residents or surveillance contractors such as PINL powers reserved for statutory security agencies. Residents help identify and report threats, while authorised agencies remain responsible for enforcement.

The theory also links pipeline security to the economic relationship between operators and host communities. It identifies employment, scholarships and community investment as benefits that should go hand in hand with residents’ responsibilities to share information, remain vigilant and facilitate access to pipeline facilities.

The framework is built around interdependence, differentiated roles, visible contribution, resilience and the enforcement of norms. It also stresses that communication, fair representation, reciprocity and accountability are necessary to sustain the arrangement.

It cited PINL’s recruitment and engagement of more than 35,000 youths across the Niger Delta to protect installations and pipeline corridors, the clearance of longstanding scholarship backlogs owed to host communities, as well as women’s empowerment and vocational training programmes in communities along the Trans-Niger Pipeline in the three states.

The study also mentioned stakeholder meetings PINL held in April 2025 and June 2026, attended by traditional rulers, Community Development Committees, youth leaders, women’s representatives, company officials and statutory agencies.

The activities provided examples of how PINL engages host communities in pipeline surveillance. The study examined them against its proposed framework, assessing how community participation and representation could help prevent pipeline theft, vandalism and production disruptions.

The study also outlined a nine-stage process known as the Weaver Operational Cycle, covering identification, assignment, engagement, listening, verification, action, reporting, review and adaptation.

Under the cycle, information received from communities must be professionally verified before action is taken. Operators are also expected to give feedback to residents who provide information and review their procedures to determine what worked and whether any groups were excluded.

The model reserves decisions and enforcement actions for competent management, regulators or statutory security agencies. Here, communities contribute information and local vigilance but do not assume the responsibilities of those authorised to enforce the law.

The June 2026 attack on the TNP at Odau in Rivers State showed how important PINL’s relationship with host communities can be during security incidents. Following the attack, the company held meetings with community leaders, youth representatives and statutory security agencies.

The discussions focused on improving communication, sharing information and coordinating recovery efforts.

The incident reinforced the need for regular communication between PINL and host communities, particularly when pipeline infrastructure comes under attack.

PINL’s relationship with host communities has also featured in the debate over pipeline surveillance contracts. In 2026, petitions to the National Assembly called for the contracts to be distributed among oil-producing communities, while other regional leaders and parliamentary panels backed continuity and central coordination.

On October 13, 2026, the National Assembly passed a vote of confidence in PINL, citing the company’s operational gains, community empowerment programmes and the absence of evidence to support allegations against it.

The debate touched on community representation in pipeline surveillance contracts and how the economic benefits are distributed among oil-producing communities.

Lawmakers commended PINL for engaging more than 35,600 local youths as pipeline surveillance guards, noting the jobs created and the contribution to stability in the Niger Delta.

Also acknowledged were the company’s interventions in host communities, including more than 5,000 undergraduate and postgraduate scholarships, skills training for 4,000 women and flood relief efforts across Rivers State.

The paper warned that community engagement must be properly organised to ensure that its benefits reach different groups. It said that, without such arrangements, benefits could become concentrated among a small group of local elites and leave other sections of host communities without an effective voice.

It also compared PINL’s approach with that of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, noting that the same model could apply to both companies. But it stressed that having locals involved in pipeline security is not enough. Communities must have clearly defined roles, see the benefits of their involvement and have a way to hold those responsible accountable.

The paper further situated the model within the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 and the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission’s framework for Host Community Development Trusts. It argued that community participation in pipeline surveillance must operate within the law and support, rather than replace, the work of security agencies.

The paper recommends that pipeline surveillance firms make community engagement a regular part of their operations rather than treat it as a corporate social responsibility project.

It also calls for formal agreements to sustain cooperation even when community leadership changes or security challenges arise.

*Olu wrote in from Abuja.

title: Telcos adopt equipment reuse to reduce emissions
description:
Telecom operators are increasingly adopting equipment reuse and refurbishment to reduce network investment costs, limit waste and cut emissions as the industry faces pressure to meet its net-zero target by 2050.
The shift is moving operators away from the traditional practice of replacing equipment
content:
Telecom operators are increasingly adopting equipment reuse and refurbishment to reduce network investment costs, limit waste and cut emissions as the industry faces pressure to meet its net-zero target by 2050.

The shift is moving operators away from the traditional practice of replacing equipment during network upgrades towards extending the lifespan of existing infrastructure, according to a Research Analyst at GSMA Intelligence, Muskan Gadodia.

In an article published on the GSMA website, Gadodia reported that the world’s 10 largest mobile network operators by subscriber base had introduced or supported more than 500 unconventional sustainability initiatives since 2020, either independently or through partnerships.

She identified equipment reuse, energy management, smarter procurement, redesigned network sites, environmental restoration and community clean-energy partnerships as six areas in which operators were expanding their sustainability efforts beyond conventional measures.

Under the equipment reuse approach, Telefónica’s MAIA platform and Orange’s OSCAR programme are helping to extend the lifespan of network equipment through reuse and refurbishment. According to Gadodia, the initiatives can reduce waste, lower capital requirements and mitigate supply-chain risks.

The development is also drawing equipment manufacturers into operators’ sustainability programmes. Orange’s OSCAR programme, for instance, has established a formal refurbishment partnership with Nokia, reflecting the growing role of suppliers in efforts to extend the useful life of telecommunications infrastructure.

Gadodia said achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 remained one of the industry’s biggest challenges, despite operators’ investments in network efficiency and renewable energy.

“Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 remains one of the telecom industry’s biggest challenges. Most mobile network operators are pursuing this goal through traditional measures such as improving network energy efficiency and increasing the use of renewable energy,” the analyst wrote.

Those measures alone might not be sufficient to close the industry’s remaining emissions gap, prompting operators to explore additional initiatives involving infrastructure, energy management and environmental restoration.

The analysis also highlighted efforts to turn telecommunications infrastructure into energy assets. Finland’s Elisa is using backup batteries at base stations in a virtual power plant model to support electricity grid balancing, while Deutsche Telekom is deploying waste heat from network facilities.

Other operators are incorporating environmental considerations into procurement decisions. Telefónica, for example, has introduced internal carbon pricing into its procurement processes, taking into account energy consumption, emissions and lifetime operating costs alongside purchase prices.

In Africa, Airtel Africa’s lean-site model in Nigeria was cited as an example of how operators are redesigning network infrastructure to reduce operational requirements. Japan’s NTT DOCOMO also operates a self-powered hydropower base station.

The sustainability drive extends to environmental monitoring and community energy projects. Orange Business and Tēnaka are collaborating on coral reef monitoring, while Vodafone has an environmental monitoring initiative in Scotland. In Kenya, Safaricom’s partnership with Sistema.bio is helping farmers access biodigesters through mobile-enabled payments and loyalty mechanisms.

The GSMA’s Mobile Net Zero report showed that the mobile industry’s operational emissions fell by eight per cent between 2019 and 2023, even as data traffic quadrupled. However, the industry needs to reduce emissions by 7.5 per cent annually by 2030, more than twice the average annual rate achieved so far, to reach net zero by 2050.

Gadodia said the unconventional initiatives were designed to complement, rather than replace, network modernisation and renewable energy adoption, as operators seek to reduce emissions across their wider operations and supply chains.

title: Nigerian passengers stranded as US flight disruptions persist
description:
Travel plans of hundreds of Nigerian travellers have been disrupted following widespread flight cancellations in the United States triggered by a nationwide air traffic control ground stop since Friday.
 The disruption, which affected thousands of flights across the US, has continued to take a toll
content:
Travel plans of hundreds of Nigerian travellers have been disrupted following widespread flight cancellations in the United States triggered by a nationwide air traffic control ground stop since Friday.

 The disruption, which affected thousands of flights across the US, has continued to take a toll on international aviation operations, leaving passengers travelling from Nigeria to the US, as well as those scheduled to return to Nigeria, grappling with delays, cancellations and uncertainty.

Findings by The PUNCH showed that several Nigerian passengers scheduled to travel to the US over the weekend were unable to embark on their journeys as planned, with some having to abandon their trips temporarily or postpone their flights until airlines could restore normal operations.

 Some perssengers temporarily spent hours within the airport terminal while some others checked into a hotel around the airport with the thought that the disruptions would only last for a day.

A passenger, Sola Aina, who spoke with our correspondent on Sunday, said he had been forced to return home after spending days waiting for his flight to be rescheduled.

 “I just have to return home today. I have come for a Friday flight before we heard of the troubles in the U.S, I have to sleep in a hotel since Friday believing that the issues would be sorted before Sunday night, but this is almost 7:00pm again now.

 “I have ordered a cab. I have to return to Ibadan. It’s very painful but I don’t have an option,” he said.

Another passenger, Faruq Akinwale, said the disruption had affected his plans to return home urgently, as his wife and sick child were in the US.

 “I have a sick child with my wife in the U.S and I need to return home urgently, but what do I do? But I understand that no one can be blamed for this, but I will only appeal that everyone concerned should please hasten up whatever they are doing, I pray God help them,” he said.

 A mother of two, Mrs Aderemi, also expressed disappointment over the situation, saying she and her family had been left with little choice but to return home.

 “We will just return home, the situation is just understandable even though it’s painful,” she said.

 Similarly, another passenger, Charles Adekunle, said the disruption had affected his travel plans, although he did not disclose whether he intended to reschedule his trip.

 The situation has also affected passengers travelling from the US to Nigeria, particularly those booked on international services connecting major American cities to Lagos and Abuja.

 Airlines operating flights between Nigeria and the US, either directly or through connecting routes, include Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines, Emirates, Virgin Atlantic and British Airways, among others.

 Although the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the nationwide ground stop on Saturday evening, airlines have continued to battle operational challenges, including the repositioning of aircraft and flight crews displaced by the disruption.

 An update published on Delta Air Lines’ website on Saturday indicated that the carrier was still working to restore normal operations following the FAA-mandated ground stop, which lasted more than four hours.

 The airline said passengers scheduled to travel between 13 and 15 November, 2026, could change their bookings without paying additional charges.

 It also encouraged customers with flexible travel arrangements to move their flights to Monday, 16 November, or later, warning that passengers travelling over the weekend should expect delays and further schedule adjustments.

 Delta said, “Delta continues to restore operations following an FAA-mandated nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, November 13. Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft.

 “Taking care of customers remains our focus, and we continue to offer flexible rebooking options to change flights at no extra cost. Customers who have flexible travel plans are encouraged to move their flights to Monday, Nov. 16 or later.

 “If you are traveling on Saturday, please allow extra time and check the Delta app or delta.com for the latest flight status and travel information. Delta will provide customers with as much notice as possible about changes to flight schedules. When a cancellation does occur, Delta will automatically rebook customers to the next best itinerary.”

 Meanwhile, the Donald Trump administration has warned that disruptions to air travel across the United States could persist until Monday, extending the wait for a full return to normal operations.

 Hundreds more flights were cancelled on Sunday, raising concerns about the scale of the disruption in the world’s largest economy, which has one of the busiest aviation networks globally.

 US officials attributed Friday’s disruption to faulty work carried out during an upgrade of air traffic control communication cables.

 President Donald Trump broke his silence on the crisis on Sunday, blaming the previous administration of Joe Biden for the state of the country’s air traffic control infrastructure.

 The FAA chief, Bryan Bedford, had said on Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans affected by the disruption would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.

 However, Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, said on Sunday that the restoration of normal operations would take longer because aircraft and flight crews had been displaced during the disruption.

title: AU pushes joint action to recover stolen African assets
description:
The African Union is seeking stronger cooperation among member states to improve the recovery of stolen assets and ensure that proceeds recovered from corruption are used for the benefit of citizens across the continent.
The Director of Special Services at the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other
content:
The African Union is seeking stronger cooperation among member states to improve the recovery of stolen assets and ensure that proceeds recovered from corruption are used for the benefit of citizens across the continent.

The Director of Special Services at the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission, Hassan Mohamed, disclosed this in a statement on Sunday ahead of an African asset recovery meeting.

Mohamed, who is also the Chairman of the Local Organising Committee for the event, said asset recovery had become an integral part of the global fight against corruption, requiring countries to harmonise their approaches and strengthen collaboration.

He said the meeting would provide an opportunity for African countries to share experiences, discuss recovery efforts and develop common strategies for tackling corruption.

“All over the world, asset recovery has become an integral part of the fight against corruption.

“It is to be sure, to ensure that what was recovered is put to use for the benefit of the generality of the masses. That is an aspect of the fight against corruption, which the African Union is advancing,” he said.

Mohamed explained that the initiative was not necessarily driven by concerns over the handling of recovered assets but by the need to ensure that such assets served the public interest.

He said the meeting would also enable participating countries to examine practical approaches to asset recovery and strengthen their collective response to the challenges associated with the process.

“The purpose of the programme is to harmonise the fight against corruption, especially now that asset recovery has become an integral part of what we do, of what anti-corruption agencies do all over the world.

“So here is to synergise, synthesise, come up with strategies, common ways to deal with this menace. Essentially, that’s what we’re doing,” he said.

The ICPC official also pledged that the commission would continue to disclose information about assets recovered by the agency, including their status, to promote transparency and accountability.

“Definitely, ICPC will do that. Nothing is hidden. It’s a public document. Anything recovered is for the public. And so, ICPC will definitely declare anything and whatever has been recovered,” he said.

He, however, declined to provide figures on assets recovered in Nigeria ahead of the meeting, saying he did not have the details available at the time of the briefing.

Mohamed said participating delegates would also have the opportunity to visit locations where some recovered assets were being put to use in Nigeria.

He added that the meeting would bring together representatives from across the continent, with about 52 to 54 African countries expected to participate.

Mohammed said the forum’s maiden General Assembly, scheduled to hold in Abuja from November 17 to 20, would provide an opportunity for African countries to develop practical strategies for addressing the challenges confronting asset recovery institutions.

He said participants would review progress in implementing the Common African Position on Asset Recovery, strengthen institutional collaboration and adopt governance instruments and strategic action plans.

He added that the meeting would also examine gaps in national and continental frameworks and identify ways of improving cooperation in the recovery and repatriation of illicitly acquired assets.

The post AU pushes joint action to recover stolen African assets appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Yayi warns against attacks on APC candidates, billboards
description:
The 2027 All Progressives Congress governorship candidate for Ogun State and senator representing Ogun West, Solomon Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, has warned against attacks on APC candidates and the destruction of their campaign materials.
Adeola declared that the ruling party would no longer to
content:
The 2027 All Progressives Congress governorship candidate for Ogun State and senator representing Ogun West, Solomon Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, has warned against attacks on APC candidates and the destruction of their campaign materials.

Adeola declared that the ruling party would no longer tolerate political violence, the destruction of campaign billboards and other acts of intimidation against its candidates and supporters.

The senator, according to a statement issued by his Special Adviser on Media, Kayode Odunaro, on Sunday, stated this during the inauguration of 357 ward and local government coordinators of the APC across the state in Yewa South Local Government Area.

The inauguration and distribution of vehicles were witnessed by the Ogun State Deputy Governor, Noimot Salako-Oyedele; former deputy governors, Salmot Badru and Segun Adesegun; Minister of State for Health, Dr Kunle Salako; Director-General of the Ogun State APC Presidential and Gubernatorial Campaign Council, Senator Lekan Mustapha; and Gboyega Isiaka, among others.

The governorship candidate called on political actors and their supporters to abide by the rule of law and embrace peaceful political participation as political campaigns progress.

“I condemn the reported attacks on APC candidates and campaign materials; it should be noted that no individual or political group has a monopoly on violence.

“Nobody has a monopoly on violence. Stoning candidates and their supporters, destroying APC candidates’ posters and their billboards will not be tolerated anymore. Nobody is above the law,” Adeola said.

“Attacks on President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Vice-President Kashim Shettima and other APC candidates must stop,” he said, warning that the party would not condone further acts of political aggression.

Adeola explained that the number of ward coordinators had been increased from 236 to 357 following a critical assessment of the peculiarities and organisational needs of various wards across the state.

He charged the newly inaugurated coordinators to work around the clock to strengthen the party’s grassroots structures, warning that anyone found engaging in activities capable of causing disaffection or undermining the APC would be removed.

The senator also cautioned the beneficiaries against personalising the vehicles and motorcycles distributed to them, stressing that the items were provided strictly for party mobilisation and official assignments.

He disclosed that plans were underway to provide Closed User Group telephone lines to the coordinators to improve communication and coordination across the state.

Adeola, who said the inauguration marked the end of his tour of the 20 local government areas of Ogun State, added that concerns and memoranda submitted by communities during the engagements would be incorporated into his economic blueprint and manifesto, tagged ITESIWAJU.

He expressed confidence that the expanded grassroots structure would help the APC achieve its target of delivering two million votes for President Tinubu in the forthcoming presidential election.

title: FirstBank Lagos Open tees off Monday
description:
The 65th edition of the FirstBank Lagos Amateur Open Golf Championship will tee off on Monday, November 16, at the Ikoyi Club 1938 Golf Section in Lagos.
The tournament runs until Sunday, November 22, and celebrates 65 unbroken years of sponsorship by FirstBank of Nigeria Limited. It is the country’
content:
The 65th edition of the FirstBank Lagos Amateur Open Golf Championship will tee off on Monday, November 16, at the Ikoyi Club 1938 Golf Section in Lagos.

The tournament runs until Sunday, November 22, and celebrates 65 unbroken years of sponsorship by FirstBank of Nigeria Limited. It is the country’s longest-running bank-sponsored golf competition.

Amateur golfers from across Nigeria and beyond will compete for top honours, along with invited professionals, especially former winners now playing on the PGA of Nigeria Tour. The total prize money is N34.5m.

The championship is recognised by the World Amateur Golf Ranking, so participants will also have the chance to earn international ranking points.

Action begins on Monday with the Search4Stars Caddies Tournament, an opening-day event celebrating the contributions of caddies. The Championship Kitty follows on Wednesday, November 18, and the Corporate Golf Challenge for Charity takes place on Thursday, November 19, where corporate teams will compete to support community impact initiatives.

The main 54-hole championship starts on Friday, November 20, with the first round. The second round is on Saturday, November 21, alongside youth coaching clinics designed to nurture aspiring young golfers. The tournament ends with the final round and a closing trophy presentation on Sunday, November 22.

Beyond golf, FirstBank supports sport through its first@sport initiatives. It has sponsored the Georgian Polo Cup at the Kaduna Polo Club for more than 105 years and the Dala Hard Court Tennis Championship in Kano for 35 years.

It also backs the E1 Lagos GP, the Elephant Girls, who compete in the NBBF League, and the Elephants Boys, who play in the lower-tier Nigerian football league.

title: Golf: 19-year-old Okoko wins CIO title with record score
description:
Nigeria’s 19-year-old golf sensation, Godwin Okoko, has stormed to a historic victory at the seventh CIO Golf Classic, posting a record-breaking 22-under-par total at the Python Golf Club in Port Harcourt, Rivers State.
The rising star delivered a commanding performance across the four-day champions
content:
Nigeria’s 19-year-old golf sensation, Godwin Okoko, has stormed to a historic victory at the seventh CIO Golf Classic, posting a record-breaking 22-under-par total at the Python Golf Club in Port Harcourt, Rivers State.

The rising star delivered a commanding performance across the four-day championship, carding rounds of 67, 63, 65 and 71 for a remarkable total of 266, shattering the three-year-old course record by four strokes.

Okoko’s triumph represents another significant milestone in his rapidly advancing professional career and further underscores the potential of Nigerian professional golf talent on the continent.

“I have been looking forward to moments like this since my career started, and I am very delighted that things are coming together for me,” an elated Okoko said after his victory.

His exceptional performance was highlighted by a stunning nine-under-par 63 in the second round, which laid the foundation for his record-breaking achievement. He subsequently maintained his advantage against a strong international field to claim one of the most prestigious titles on Nigeria’s professional golf calendar.

Chairman of Keeves Global Leasing, sponsors of the championship, Chief Ikenna Okafor, described the youngster’s achievement as impressive and a fitting climax to an event that continues to raise the standard of professional golf in Nigeria.

“Okoko’s record score puts the icing on the effort and growth this seventh CIO Classic has offered. He is an ambitious and talented player who is bold enough to carry the hopes and aspirations of Nigeria golf supporters and investors who are thinking of how to support golf in Nigeria,” Okafor said.

The victory also carries significant implications beyond the championship’s ₦100 million total prize purse, placing Okoko in pole position on the Safari Tour rankings and strengthening his prospects of qualifying for the 2027 Magical Kenya Open.

Ghana’s Vincent Torgah mounted a spirited challenge but finished two strokes behind the champion at 20-under-par, while Zambia’s Sydney Wemba secured third place at 15-under-par.

Nigeria’s Gift Willy and Uganda’s Ronald Rugumayo shared fourth place at 10-under-par, while Samuel Emmanuel Odey, Sunday Olapade and Zimbabwe’s Samuel Njoroge tied for sixth at nine-under-par.

Kenya’s Nuru Mollel and Nigeria’s Francis Epe completed the top 10, sharing ninth position at seven-under-par

title: Lawani, Saliu triumph at 2026 Elizabeth Wuraola Ojo tourney
description:
Abiodun Muyiwa Lawani of Nimbar Golf Club, Ondo City, and Adenike Saliu of Ikeja Golf Club won the men’s and ladies’ overall titles, respectively, at the 2026 Elizabeth Wuraola Ojo Toyota Golf Tournament.
The tournament drew golfers from various clubs to the Smokin Hills Golf Resort, Ilara-Mokin, On
content:
Abiodun Muyiwa Lawani of Nimbar Golf Club, Ondo City, and Adenike Saliu of Ikeja Golf Club won the men’s and ladies’ overall titles, respectively, at the 2026 Elizabeth Wuraola Ojo Toyota Golf Tournament.

The tournament drew golfers from various clubs to the Smokin Hills Golf Resort, Ilara-Mokin, Ondo State.

Lawani, playing off handicap 19, returned a gross score of 81 and a net score of 62 to take the men’s crown. Saliu, off handicap 22, won the ladies’ title with a net 66 from a gross 88.

In the men’s net category, Fagboyibo Fass was second with a net 65, from a gross 87 off handicap 22. Seun Olagoke also returned a net 65, from a gross 90 off handicap 25.

Isaac Shedowo won the men’s veterans category, off handicap 25, with a gross 99 and a net 74. Lincoln Ojo was second with the same net 74, from a gross 100 off handicap 25.

In the men’s gross category, Tunji Ojuolape won with 76 off handicap seven, while Kewani Amusan was second with 81 off handicap three.

Toyin Olusegun was runner-up in the ladies’ net category with a net 67, from a gross 88 off handicap 21. Halima Agbeniyi was third with a net 68, from a gross 96 off handicap 28.

Diana Osmond of Ikeja Golf Club won the ladies’ gross category with 78, with Grace Yusuf, who plays off handicap eight, in second place.

Ropo Olaofe won the ladies’ veterans category with a net 75, from a gross 111 off handicap 36. Chichi was second with a net 78, from a gross 87 off handicap nine.

Lawani, the captain of Nimbar Golf Club, described his win as an act of grace. He said his golfing career began at Smokin Hills and thanked the resort’s proprietor, Chief Michael Ade-Ojo, for providing world-class facilities.

“I feel so great that I won today. I started my golfing career here at Smokin Hills Golf Club, but I am now a member of Nimbar Golf Club, Ondo. Smokin Hills is a world-class golf resort. I want to thank our dear father, Chief Michael Ade-Ojo, for this monumental infrastructure. It was a great task playing on the Smokin Hills golf course, but thank God I eventually emerged a winner,” he said.

“I see this victory as a privilege and grace. It is not just about expertise, training or the time you have put into the game. It is God’s grace, and I do not take it for granted. I also appreciate the organisers for making the tournament a success.”

The post Lawani, Saliu triumph at 2026 Elizabeth Wuraola Ojo tourney appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Lekki residents threaten monthly protests over power outages
description: Residents of Orchid Road, Lekki, Lagos State, have threatened to stage monthly protests over persistent electricity outages, accusing Eko Electricity Distribution Company and the Transmission Company of Nigeria of failing to provide reliable power supply despite regular payment of electricity bills.
content:
Residents of Orchid Road, Lekki, Lagos State, have threatened to stage monthly protests over persistent electricity outages, accusing Eko Electricity Distribution Company and the Transmission Company of Nigeria of failing to provide reliable power supply despite regular payment of electricity bills.

 The residents, under the aegis of the Lekki Conservation Estate Community Development Area, took to the streets at Monife Roundabout over the weekend, displaying placards to express their frustration over what they described as months of darkness.

 Some of the placards read, “We Pay Premium Rates But Get Zero Reliability!”, “Orchid Road Band B = Band Nothing”, “Eko Power is a Charade”, “Orchid Road Deserves a Power Station” and “TCN Needs to Be Unbundled.”

 The protesters, comprising landlords, tenants, business owners and community leaders, said the prolonged outages had disrupted businesses, increased household expenses and forced estates to rely heavily on diesel-powered generators.

 Speaking during the protest, the President of LECECODA, Bode Akinwande, said the community had endured poor electricity supply for more than four months, despite repeated engagements with Eko DisCo.

 “For the last four months, our community has been without meaningful power supply, and our repeated efforts to resolve the matter through dialogue have yielded no result,” he said.

 Akinwande said the community received virtually no electricity throughout October, despite residents continuing to receive electricity bills running into millions of naira.

 “Let us take the month of October as an example. In the month of October, we did not receive two hours of supply cumulatively, and unfortunately, members of this community in various estates have received bills in the millions. This is not acceptable to us,” he stated.

 He explained that Orchid Road was a 7.5-kilometre corridor in Lekki, housing about 200 residential estates, as well as schools, restaurants, shopping malls, supermarkets, churches and mosques.

 According to him, the community receives electricity through the Maroko 33kV feeder at Ajah but has no dedicated injection substation to serve its growing population.

 He alleged that the feeder trips daily, sometimes at the slightest threat of rainfall, leaving residents without electricity for several days.

 “In recent weeks, supply has been restored for as little as two minutes after intervals of four or five days without power,” he said.

 The community leader also accused Eko DisCo and TCN of shifting responsibility for the poor supply between themselves, leaving consumers to bear the consequences.

 Akinwande said the association had formally written to the acting Managing Director of Eko DisCo, Sharifat Adegbenro, on October 20, 2026, requesting a meeting to address the situation.

 He, however, expressed disappointment that the company only responded after learning of the planned protest.

 Akinwande warned that the residents would return to the streets every month until there was an appreciable improvement in electricity supply.

 He said, “If we do not see stable power supply, next month we are going to gather again to let members of the community and Nigeria as a whole know what they have done. So, it will be monthly until we receive an appreciable improvement in power supply to us.”

 Speaking on the economic consequences of the outages, a community stakeholder, Faith Oliver, said businesses along the corridor had suffered substantial losses, with some forced to shut down because of unreliable electricity.

 She said businesses dealing in frozen foods, restaurants, supermarkets and shopping malls had been particularly affected because of their dependence on refrigeration.

 “In terms of businesses as a whole, we have lost billions. So, many businesses here have been shut down, as they cannot even operate functionally because of low power supply,” Oliver said.

 Oliver also lamented the impact of the outages on residents’ daily lives, saying some households had been unable to pump water because of the lack of electricity.

 The immediate past president of the association, Irene Osas, said the electricity crisis had persisted for more than 10 years despite repeated engagements with the distribution company.

 Osas said the community had received several assurances and entered into agreements with the company over the years without any significant improvement in service delivery.

 Giving an indication of the financial burden on residents, Osas disclosed that his estate spent about N6m monthly on diesel to supplement electricity supply, adding that the estate now owed diesel suppliers.

 Another resident, Engineer Olosho Saheed, accused Eko DisCo of issuing estimated bills despite the availability of functioning meters in some estates.

 He said the unreliable supply had forced his estate to increase electricity charges collected from residents while also struggling to meet its diesel expenses.

 Saheed disclosed that the estate operated a 500kVA generator, which consumed between 600 and 800 litres of diesel daily.

 “We cannot continue with this. Eko Power has to do better by us, and they have to improve,” Saheed stated.

 Also speaking, the Chairman of the association’s Board of Trustees, Taiwo Enilolobo, questioned the continued billing of residents despite the poor electricity supply.

 Enilolobo said between 95 and 98 per cent of residents along the corridor paid their electricity bills as and when due.

 The association called on Eko DisCo to restore electricity supply in line with the community’s Band B classification or review its billing to reflect the actual service delivered.

 It also demanded a technical audit of the Maroko 33kV feeder, a time-bound plan to address persistent tripping and a commitment to constructing a dedicated injection substation for the Orchid Road corridor.

 The residents further urged TCN’s Ajah Transmission Station to explain the prolonged outages on the feeder and work with Eko DisCo to restore stable supply.

 They also called on the regulators to investigate the electricity service delivered to the community against its Band B classification over the past four months.

 Eko DisCo had yet to respond to messages and calls from our correspondent seeking its reaction to the allegations as of the time of filing this report.

The post Lekki residents threaten monthly protests over power outages appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: FG raises W’Bank power loan to $1.25bn
description:
The Federal Government is seeking an additional $500m loan from the World Bank to expand its renewable energy programme, a move that would raise the bank’s total financing for the project to $1.25bn amid persistent electricity shortages and frequent power outages across Nigeria.
The proposed financi
content:
The Federal Government is seeking an additional $500m loan from the World Bank to expand its renewable energy programme, a move that would raise the bank’s total financing for the project to $1.25bn amid persistent electricity shortages and frequent power outages across Nigeria.

The proposed financing will add to the $750m previously approved by the World Bank for the Nigeria Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up project, known as DARES, which is being implemented by the Rural Electrification Agency.

According to a World Bank Project Information Document obtained by The PUNCH on Sunday, the additional $500m loan is scheduled for consideration by the bank’s Board of Executive Directors on 18 December, 2026, three years after the original financing was approved.

“This is a proposed Additional Financing in the amount of $500m for the Nigeria Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up Project. DARES was approved on December 14, 2023 and reached effectiveness on November 15, 2024. The Project Development Objective is to increase access to electricity services for households, public institutions, and micro, small and medium enterprises with private sector-led distributed renewable energy generation,” the document read.

The document, prepared on 13 November, 2026, showed that the government intends to expand electricity access to households, businesses, schools, healthcare facilities and underserved communities through solar-powered systems and mini-grids.

The bank explained that the additional financing would accelerate the deployment of renewable energy infrastructure, particularly in communities that remain disconnected from the national electricity grid.

It said, “The proposed AF will enable the scale-up and expansion of electricity services through mini grids and standalone solar systems, while sustaining the momentum of private sector-led access delivery.”

The fresh borrowing proposal comes amid persistent electricity supply challenges in Nigeria, where households and businesses continue to experience outages and depend heavily on petrol and diesel generators.

The World Bank estimated that 87.2 million Nigerians lacked electricity access in 2024, despite improvements in the national electrification rate over the preceding decade.

According to the report, electricity access increased from 52.5 per cent in 2015 to 61.2 per cent in 2024. However, population growth meant that the absolute number of people without electricity had barely declined.

The situation was worse in rural communities, where only 32.9 per cent of residents had access to electricity, leaving more than two-thirds without power.

The bank observed, “Nigeria continues to face a significant electricity access gap despite recent progress.”

It added that the existing DARES financing was designed to provide electricity connections to more than 18.8 million people, representing only about 22 per cent of the country’s electricity access deficit.

The report estimated that Nigeria would require approximately $23bn to achieve universal electricity access by 2030, with distributed renewable energy solutions potentially providing electricity to more than 60 million people at a lower cost than conventional alternatives.

The latest proposal follows the World Bank’s approval of the original $750m DARES financing on 14 December, 2023, during the administration of President Bola Tinubu.

The project became effective on 15 November, 2024, about 11 months after approval, with the objective of expanding electricity access through private sector-led renewable energy investments.

The existing financing comprises $600m in shorter-maturity loans from the International Development Association and another $150m in IDA credit.

Under the proposed expansion, the IDA credit component would increase from $150m to $650m, while the $600m shorter-maturity loan component would remain unchanged.

This would bring the total World Bank financing to $1.25bn if the additional request receives board approval.

An analysis of the financing arrangements showed that the overall DARES project cost would also increase from $2.06bn to $2.94bn, representing an additional $880.2m or 42.71 per cent.

The proposed increase comprises $500m from the World Bank, $116.2m from the French Development Agency and $264m in expected commercial financing.

Consequently, total commercial financing under the programme is projected to rise from $1.028bn to $1.292bn, while contributions from other development partners would bring total co-financing from those sources to $350m.

The financing package also includes $193.8m from the Japan International Cooperation Agency, $49.1m in trust fund resources contributed through a United States Department of Justice-supported fund and $40m in other development partner financing.

The World Bank’s Country Director for Nigeria, Taimur Samad, endorsed the latest project document on 13 November, 2026, while the appraisal date was listed as 23 October.

Meanwhile, an analysis of the World Bank’s transaction records for the existing project showed that $128.44m had been disbursed from the original $750m financing commitment, representing approximately 17.13 per cent.

The records, covering transactions up to 22 October 2026, indicated that the disbursements were recorded against one of the financing agreements supporting the project.

This implies that approximately $621.56m, representing 82.87 per cent of the original financing, had yet to be recorded as disbursed in the transaction data reviewed.

The original financing was divided into three commitments of $350m, $250m and $150m, approved on 14 December, 2023.

The position raises questions about the pace of financial implementation, particularly as the Federal Government seeks additional borrowing before the existing financing has been fully utilised.

However, the World Bank explained that access to some of the funds depended on the achievement of performance conditions, including regulatory reforms and institutional improvements.

According to the report, $300m had been unlocked after the government met two performance-based conditions.

The post FG raises W’Bank power loan to $1.25bn appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Uganda woos Dangote for oil refinery, fertiliser projects
description:
Uganda has approached the Dangote Group to invest in its proposed billion-dollar oil refinery, fertiliser and salt production projects as the East African country seeks to transform its natural resources into finished products, create jobs and reduce dependence on imports.
 The country made the inve
content:
Uganda has approached the Dangote Group to invest in its proposed billion-dollar oil refinery, fertiliser and salt production projects as the East African country seeks to transform its natural resources into finished products, create jobs and reduce dependence on imports.

 The country made the investment pitch during a visit to the Dangote Petroleum Refinery & Petrochemicals and Dangote Fertiliser Limited in Lagos by a delegation led by its Minister of Energy and Mineral Development, Dr Monica Musenero Masanza, and Minister of State for Finance, Planning and Economic Development (Privatisation and Investment), Hajjat Amina Mukalazi.

According to a statement on Sunday, the ministers called on Africa’s richest industrialist, Aliko Dangote, to partner with Uganda in developing its petroleum and mineral resources, particularly through the proposed 60,000-barrel-per-day refinery in the Hoima area.

They also identified opportunities in fertiliser blending, phosphate processing and salt manufacturing, expressing the government’s readiness to support the proposed investments and remove obstacles to their implementation.

President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Dangote, received the delegation alongside senior executives of the group, including the Group Vice President, Devakumar Edwin.

Presenting Uganda’s proposals, Mukalazi invited Dangote to take a leading role in the planned refinery, describing the project as a major industrial priority for the country.

She said the group’s experience in engineering, construction and operating large industrial facilities would be valuable to the project.

“You have shown that an African company can build world-scale industry in Africa and run it by Africans themselves,” she said.

Mukalazi noted that the refinery could complement the Dangote Group’s proposed refinery in Lamu, Kenya, with the Ugandan facility serving inland markets while the coastal project supplied maritime and coastal markets.

She, however, acknowledged that the estimates presented by the delegation would require technical assessment by Dangote’s team.

The minister stated that Uganda’s crude oil, phosphate and salt deposits offered opportunities for investments that can be connected through shared infrastructure and distribution networks.

“Our crude, our phosphate, our salt are waiting to be turned into fuel, fertilisers and chemicals here in Africa and in Uganda by Africans,” Mukalazi said.

She also invited Dangote to visit Uganda for further discussions, assuring him that the government would support the proposed partnership and address investment bottlenecks.

“Uganda needs Dangote, and now is the right time. Our country is ready and moving rapidly towards industrialisation.

“He (Dangote) would bring investment, technology and opportunities for local participation, as we have seen here today. He has demonstrated what is possible elsewhere, and we believe he can do the same in Uganda,“ she noted.

Mukalazi said the proposed investments would create opportunities for skills development, employment and local businesses, particularly among young people.

Also speaking, Uganda’s Minister of Energy and Mineral Development, Dr Musenero, said the delegation visited the facilities to learn from Dangote’s industrial experience and explore practical areas of collaboration in the country’s petroleum and fertiliser industries.

She identified fertiliser production as a major investment opportunity, explaining that Uganda had mineral resources suitable for manufacturing fertilisers but had not been successful in converting them into finished products.

In his remarks, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery & Petrochemicals, David Bird, said the presence of the two ministers demonstrated Uganda’s commitment to exploring an industrial partnership with the group.

He said the country had significant natural resources and human capital, alongside the political commitment required to pursue industrialisation.

“Uganda has incredible natural resources and human capital. As both ministers have expressed during this visit, there is also no shortage of ambition or political will to pursue industrialisation,” he said.

The post Uganda woos Dangote for oil refinery, fertiliser projects appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: FCMB finances 60,000-tonne plastic recycling plant
description:
First City Monument Bank has provided N40bn in machinery and working-capital financing to Polysmart Packaging Limited for a plastic recycling plant with an annual production capacity of 60,000 tonnes in Ileke town, Ogun State.
A statement from the bank on Sunday said that the facility, commissioned
content:
First City Monument Bank has provided N40bn in machinery and working-capital financing to Polysmart Packaging Limited for a plastic recycling plant with an annual production capacity of 60,000 tonnes in Ileke town, Ogun State.

A statement from the bank on Sunday said that the facility, commissioned on 29 October, will convert recovered post-consumer plastic waste into food-grade recycled polyethylene terephthalate materials for manufacturers.

Described by Polysmart as Africa’s largest plastic recycling plant, the investment is expected to strengthen local packaging production, support plastic-waste recovery and reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported raw materials.

Speaking at the commissioning ceremony, Minister of Environment, Balarabe Lawal, said the facility would improve Nigeria’s capacity to recover and recycle plastic waste while supporting the country’s environmental sustainability objectives.

Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, described the investment as a demonstration of Nigerian enterprise, innovation and the opportunities created by a supportive investment environment.

FCMB Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Yemisi Edun, said the bank’s support reflected its commitment to financing businesses that combine industrial development with environmental responsibility and economic opportunities.

“At FCMB, we believe that financing sustainable businesses is essential to building a resilient economy and securing long-term shared prosperity. By converting recovered plastic into new products, this plant shows how manufacturing and environmental responsibility can work together,” Edun said.

“Polysmart embodies our commitment to sustainable manufacturing practices, environmental sustainability and wealth creation, reflected in our ₦40 billion in funding for machinery and working capital.”

Polysmart Group Managing Director, Wasiu Balogun, said the investment demonstrated the capacity of Nigerian businesses to develop recycling infrastructure that serves local industries and creates opportunities across the waste-recovery chain.

“This is climate action made in Nigeria. The investment demonstrates the capacity of Nigerian businesses to develop world-class recycling infrastructure,” Balogun said.

He said the facility would process up to 100,000 tonnes of mixed plastics annually at full capacity, equivalent to about 6.5 billion bottles.

Balogun added that the operation was expected to generate about 1,000 direct jobs and more than 50,000 indirect jobs across plastic collection, aggregation, transportation and processing.

He also acknowledged FCMB’s longstanding support, saying the bank’s financing and partnership had been instrumental in Polysmart’s growth and expansion.

Polysmart estimates that Nigeria consumes about 600,000 tonnes of virgin PET annually, creating opportunities for locally produced recycled materials to replace some imported resin.

The company projects that the facility could save Nigeria about $72m annually in foreign exchange by reducing imports of virgin resin. Founded in 2013, Polysmart Packaging Limited produces food-grade recycled PET resin and flakes from post-consumer plastic waste.

The post FCMB finances 60,000-tonne plastic recycling plant appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: NEM Insurance appoints former SEC DG to board
description:
NEM Insurance Plc has appointed former Director-General of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Mounir Gwarzo, and Adejoke Teluwo as Non-Executive Directors to its board, effective 28 October, 2026.
 The company disclosed the appointments in a notice filed with the Nigerian Exchange Limited on 9
content:
NEM Insurance Plc has appointed former Director-General of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Mounir Gwarzo, and Adejoke Teluwo as Non-Executive Directors to its board, effective 28 October, 2026.

 The company disclosed the appointments in a notice filed with the Nigerian Exchange Limited on 9 November, 2026.

 Gwarzo was appointed as an Independent Non-Executive Director, while Teluwo joined the board as a Non-Executive Director.

 Gwarzo brings more than 30 years of experience spanning capital market regulation, banking, securities, trade and commerce.

 He previously served as Executive Commissioner in charge of Operations at the SEC before becoming its Director-General.

 His career also includes stints at the Ministry of Trade and Commerce, the Nigerian Stock Exchange, the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria and the SEC.

 At the Federal Mortgage Bank, he served as General Manager and Regional Executive overseeing the bank’s northern operations.

 Gwarzo is currently the Chief Executive Officer of Prime Capital and Investment Limited.

 He holds a bachelor’s degree from Bayero University, Kano, and a master’s degree in Management and Leadership from Robert Kennedy College, in collaboration with York St John University, United Kingdom. He is also a fellow of the Chartered Institute of Stockbrokers.

 Teluwo, on her part, has more than 15 years of experience across regulated businesses and entrepreneurial environments, with expertise in governance, regulatory compliance, enterprise risk management and legal matters.

 She holds an LLB degree from Coventry University, United Kingdom, and previously served as Compliance Lead at Exso Focus Group in London between 2016 and 2019.

 She is currently the Founder and Managing Director of Kintsu, a professional services and workspace enterprise providing operational infrastructure and business solutions.

 NEM Insurance said the appointments would strengthen the board’s collective expertise and effectiveness, adding that it expected the new directors to contribute to the company’s strategic objectives and corporate governance standards.

 The appointments come as the insurer continues to pursue its business objectives in Nigeria’s insurance industry.

The post NEM Insurance appoints former SEC DG to board appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Sovereign Trust Insurance’s assets rise 48% to N41.78bn
description:
Sovereign Trust Insurance Plc increased its total assets by 48 per cent to N41.78bn as of September 2026, from N28.31bn at the end of December 2025, supported by growth in cash holdings, financial investments and reinsurance contract assets.
 The insurer disclosed this in its unaudited financial sta
content:
Sovereign Trust Insurance Plc increased its total assets by 48 per cent to N41.78bn as of September 2026, from N28.31bn at the end of December 2025, supported by growth in cash holdings, financial investments and reinsurance contract assets.

 The insurer disclosed this in its unaudited financial statements for the nine months ended 30 September, 2026, filed with the Nigerian Exchange.

 Cash and cash equivalents rose by 36.3 per cent to N15.94bn from N11.69bn, while investments in financial assets measured at fair value through profit or loss increased to N4.99bn from N2.07bn.

 Reinsurance contract assets recorded one of the largest increases, rising to N9.90bn from N3.95bn, representing a 150.7 per cent increase.

 The company’s statutory deposit also rose to N1.5bn from N315m, while property, plant and equipment increased to N3.08bn from N2.70bn.

 The balance sheet expansion coincided with a return to profitability, as the insurer posted a profit after tax of N1.04bn in the nine months ended September 2026, compared with a N100.53m in the corresponding period of 2025.

 Profit before tax increased to N1.23bn from N171.67m a year earlier.

 The improvement in earnings came despite a decline in insurance revenue, which fell by 21.4 per cent to N31.53bn from N40.13bn in the corresponding period of 2025.

 Insurance service expenses declined by 24.9 per cent to N13.75bn from N18.31bn, while the insurance service result stood at N1.69bn from N1.70bn.

 However, net expenses from reinsurance contracts held remained high at N16.09bn, although they declined from N20.12bn in the previous year.

 Investment returns increased to N3.64bn from N1.53bn, supported by higher investment income and fair value gains on financial assets.

 Shareholders’ funds rose to N21.71bn from N15.66bn at the end of December 2025, partly supported by N5.02bn raised through the issuance of share capital during the period.

 Insurance contract liabilities also increased to N14.09bn from N6.50bn, reflecting higher obligations associated with the company’s insurance business.

 Sovereign Trust Insurance provides general insurance and risk management services to individual and corporate customers.

title: GOXI combines high claims payments with community development drive
description: GOXI Microinsurance Company Limited is combining insurance claims settlement with community development initiatives, having paid N160.65m to policyholders between January and July 2026 while stepping up interventions in environmental sustainability, women’s empowerment and support for vulnerable gro
content:
GOXI Microinsurance Company Limited is combining insurance claims settlement with community development initiatives, having paid N160.65m to policyholders between January and July 2026 while stepping up interventions in environmental sustainability, women’s empowerment and support for vulnerable groups.

 The company said the claims payments provided financial relief to individuals and businesses affected by unexpected losses, reflecting the role of microinsurance in helping low-income households and small business owners protect their livelihoods.

 The latest payout adds to more than N821m in claims the insurer had previously reported paying to traders, low-income households and small business owners over six years.

 Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of GOXI Microinsurance, Shina Gbadegesin, said claims settlement remained central to the company’s mission of protecting customers against financial shocks.

 He said the value of insurance became evident when policyholders experienced losses and received financial support to recover.

 “The N160.65m paid in claims between January and July 2026 reflects our commitment to honouring our promises and providing timely relief to our policyholders. We will continue to make insurance affordable, accessible and relevant to individuals, families and small businesses,” Gbadegesin said.

 Beyond its claims obligations, the insurer has expanded its corporate social responsibility activities to address social and environmental challenges in its host communities.

 In June 2026, the company organised an environmental clean-up and waste-management awareness campaign at Alade Market in Ikeja, Lagos.

 The exercise brought together employees, traders and other community members to promote responsible waste disposal and improve environmental cleanliness in the market.

 The company also marked International Women’s Day on 9 March, 2026, by visiting three female clients and presenting them with gift items in recognition of women’s contributions to families, businesses and economic development.

 The engagement aligned with the United Nations’ 2026 International Women’s Day theme, ‘Rights. Justice. Action. For ALL Women and Girls.’

 Earlier, in October 2025, GOXI had extended its community intervention to Modupe Cole Memorial Child Care and Treatment Home in Akoka, Lagos, where it supported children and other vulnerable individuals through donations and direct engagement.

 Gbadegesin said the company’s community programmes complemented its core insurance business by addressing broader social and environmental needs.

 “For us, microinsurance and corporate social responsibility are connected by one purpose — protecting people and strengthening communities,” he said.

 He added that while claims payments helped customers recover from unexpected losses, community initiatives enabled the company to contribute to the wellbeing of vulnerable groups and the sustainability of local communities.

 The company said its interventions had helped strengthen stakeholder confidence, improve employee engagement and deepen relationships with host communities.

 GOXI Microinsurance, Nigeria’s first licensed standalone microinsurance company, provides life and non-life insurance products to low-income individuals, households, microenterprises and small businesses under the regulation of the National Insurance Commission.

The post GOXI combines high claims payments with community development drive appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
